“Then this isn’t an accident.”

The conclusion settled among them. It was not proof. Proof required records, signatures, mechanisms opened and examined. But beneath the ruined city, with survivors watching from broken windows and a Council route painted backward on the wall, certainty felt like a door beginning to unlock.

From somewhere below, the three taps sounded again.

This time Mara answered.

She struck the side of the boat with her rod: three measured blows.

No one spoke.

Far beneath them, something struck back.

chapters.name: The Unstable Lock
chapters.content:
The lock was beneath Saint Orra’s old bell, where the tower’s foundations descended into the tide district like a clenched fist.

Mara reached the maintenance vault at low water with a lamp between her teeth and a satchel of charges against her hip. The bell above had been sealed after the eastern quakes, and the tower leaned over the canal, black with soot and salt. Most of Veyr’s citizens passed beneath it without looking up.

That was the advantage of old things. People trusted whatever had been allowed to become invisible.

She brushed grit from a brass plate. Beneath it, a narrow aperture opened into the locking assembly: three nested gears, a spring housing, and the emergency release connecting the tower to the city’s warning network. The Council had replaced the visible mechanisms years ago. The lock below remained original.

“Don’t touch it.”

Tomas’s voice carried down the ladder.

Mara held her hand an inch from the gear teeth. “I wasn’t touching it.”

“You were considering touching it.”

“Then you should be grateful I’m thorough.”

He climbed into the vault, bringing cold air and wet wool with him. He was younger then, though the strain around his eyes had already become permanent. His coat had no Council insignia yet. A coil of copper wire hung over one shoulder, and a revolver rested beneath his belt.

He knelt beside her and angled the lamp toward the assembly.

The gears were green with age. A hairline crack ran through the spring housing.

“How long has that been there?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

“You inspected this last night.”

“I inspected the outer casing.”

“You said the lock was sound.”

“I said the tower could be reached through the lock.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No,” Tomas said. “It isn’t.”

Above them, Saint Orra’s bell gave a faint, involuntary groan. Dust sifted through the masonry. Mara imagined its weight traveling through the cracked stone and into the mechanism beneath their knees.

The plan lay folded in her coat: Towers Seven, Four, Nine, and Saint Orra. Four points in the city’s warning lattice. Four cuts through the Council’s silence.

They would seize the towers, splice the copper network into the public signal lines, and broadcast the evacuation orders the Council had hidden. Every district would hear which routes, trains, fuel stores, and medical wagons had been reserved for the elevated wards. The Council would have to open those routes or own the deaths in full daylight.

It was not a violent plan. That was what Mara told herself each morning while drawing it again.

The charges were for doors, not bodies. The signal relays could be disabled without killing the operators. Nessa Quill had drilled the dockworkers in restraint: no fires, no hostages, no weapons unless cornered. They would make the truth impossible to ignore.

Tomas pressed a finger beside the crack. The spring housing shifted.

“Listen,” he said.

“I can see it.”

He eased a wrench against the locking tooth and turned it a fraction. Somewhere beneath them, a mechanism clicked. Another answered higher in the tower.

Mara felt the vibration through her palm.

A third click came late.

Tomas withdrew the wrench.

“If we trip this,” he said, “the release may jam between positions.”

“Then we clear it.”

“If it jams while the bell is engaged, the counterweight could drop.”

“Into the canal.”

“Into the canal if the housing holds. If the spring fails, the weight comes through the lower shaft.”

He pointed to the stone beneath the brass plate. A narrow seam ran through it.

“Through here,” he said. “Through the vault.”

Mara looked at the seam. Above them were Vey, who had lied about his age to join them; a machinist named Pellin; and Nessa’s youngest brother, Lio, who hummed whenever he was afraid.

“Then we don’t engage the bell,” she said. “We bypass the local release.”

“The bypass is what I’m still verifying.”

“You said the design was copied from the Seven-Tower plans.”

“It was modified.”

“By whom?”

“That’s what I’m trying to find out.”

She stood, striking her shoulder against the low ceiling. The lamp flame stretched thin and blue.

“Don’t,” Tomas said.

“Don’t what?”

“Turn this into a question of courage.”

She laughed once. “The Council has built an entire city out of that confusion.”

He looked at her.

Their orders had been written in careful language. Defer repairs until the dry season. Delay disclosure until public stability could be assessed. Restrict access pending verification. Preserve essential transport.

Every sentence had been clean. Every sentence had contained a grave.

Tomas rubbed his thumb along the cracked housing. “The original lock was designed to release one tower at a time. Whoever altered it tied the emergency line into the counterweight.”

“Whoever altered it?”

“You know what that means.”

“I know what everything means when you tell me only half of it.”

“It means the Council may have made the warning system impossible to trigger safely.”

“Or impossible to trigger at all.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are we discussing whether to proceed?”

“Because knowing a trap exists is not the same as stepping into it.”

She moved toward the ladder.

“Mara.”

She stopped.

“If you set a charge here before I understand the lock, you may bring down Saint Orra.”

“Then the city will hear it.”

“No. The city will watch it fall.”

“People watch everything fall. That has never made them act.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer anyone has given me.”

She climbed to the platform. Wind struck her face, carrying the mineral stink of the drained canal. From there she saw the other towers: Seven near the foundries, Four above the tram exchange, Nine on the northern embankment. Their roofs caught the morning light before South Hook did.

Below, Nessa and the workers waited. Their faces tilted toward her. Tomas emerged a moment later, and she saw the question pass among them.

“Problem?” Nessa called.

“Maintenance issue,” Tomas said.

Mara descended three steps. “The lock is unstable.”

Nessa’s mouth tightened. “Can it be used?”

“Not safely,” Tomas said.

“Safely,” Mara repeated.

Nessa glanced between them. “Patrols are due at the foundries in less than an hour.”

“I know.”

“Then decide.”

Tomas turned toward Mara. “We decide not to gamble with the people above us.”

“The people above us are already being gambled.”

“That doesn’t give us the right to choose the stake.”

Mara descended until they stood level. “You think the Council asks permission before choosing?”

“No.”

“You think it weighs lives differently?”

“No.”

“Then what are you saying?”

“That we should not become the instrument they have named us.”

The words struck because she had already been thinking them.

For weeks, the presses had printed the split black bell beneath her name. Bellmaker. Radical engineer. Enemy of civic order. The image showed a woman with a fuse in one hand and a city burning behind her. They had never printed her face. They had no need. The shape of the story was enough.

She had wanted to laugh at it. Instead she had studied it.

The Council understood spectacle. It knew people did not need proof if they were given a figure large enough to contain their fear. It knew terror could be organized, repeated, and made useful.

Truth alone had no such discipline.

Their first attempt had proved that. They had taken only the tower rooms and tried to read the evacuation lists over a clean signal. A patrol arrived early. Guards broke Nessa’s brother’s hand. Thirty-two workers went into cells, and by evening the controlled presses called it a labor disturbance.

The city heard nothing.

No one came to the gates. No merchants halted their carts. People folded the knowledge away and went on with their work, grateful to believe survival was a private virtue.

Mara returned to the vault.

Tomas followed. “You’re not setting the Saint Orra charge.”

“I’m changing the order.”

“You said you wouldn’t touch the lock.”

“I said I wouldn’t set that charge.”

“That is not better.”

She opened the satchel and removed the shaped charges, each wrapped in oilcloth. The original design placed one at the local release and a smaller one at the signal relay. A clean interruption, followed by the broadcast splice.

Mara laid them in a row and took out her knife.

Tomas caught her wrist. “What are you doing?”

“Changing the arrangement.”

“You can’t route four towers through a damaged lock.”

“Not through the lock. Around it.”

“The old network won’t carry a simultaneous load.”

“It will if we use the maintenance return.”

“That line was decommissioned.”

“It was concealed, not removed.”

“How do you know?”

“I designed the restoration plans.”

“Before they altered them.”

“Then I’ll design around the alterations.”

He stepped between her and the satchel. “You’re not hearing me.”

“I hear you very clearly.”

“You want all four bells.”

“Yes.”

“Together.”

“Yes.”

“Even if the signal surge tears through the network?”

“The towers will ring.”

“Even if the relays overload?”

“The towers will ring.”

“Even if Saint Orra’s counterweight drops?”

Mara looked toward the brass plate and the darkness below the foundation.

“Then it will fall,” she said.

Tomas’s expression changed—not with anger, but recognition. He had found the place in her where the decision had already been made.

“You think fear will save them,” he said.

“I think fear is the only language the Council has taught the city to understand.”

“And if the fear reaches everyone before the truth does?”

“Then they will move.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere the Council has told them they cannot go.”

“That isn’t a plan.”

“It is more of one than waiting for permission.”

He seized the satchel. Mara grabbed the opposite strap. For several seconds they stood locked over the charges, neither willing to yield. Above them, the old bell groaned.

Tomas released the satchel first—not surrender, only refusal to make the struggle physical.

“You’re making yourself the story,” he said.

“No. They already made me the story.”

She rewired the charges by hand, stripping insulation with her teeth. The new arrangement was ugly but direct: one pulse through the maintenance return, split at the central junction, all four tower relays receiving the same command. There would be no staggered warning, no sequence for operators to interrupt. The whole city would hear the alarm as one impossible event.

A mass flight, she thought. People pouring from the lower wards before the Council could chain the gates. Hospital routes breached by workers, rail platforms seized by families, northern checkpoints overwhelmed by the bodies they had meant to exclude.

The Council would have to open the city or kill it in public.

Her hands had stopped shaking.

Tomas stood near the ladder, watching.

“You’ll have one chance to stop this,” she said.

“Will I?”

“If the signal fails.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

Mara closed the satchel.

“Then Veyr will finally listen.”

She carried the charges up into the pale morning. At the tower’s base, Nessa waited with the others. Mara gave instructions without looking at Tomas: Seven first, then Four, then Nine. Saint Orra last. No one was to touch the bell housing. No one was to wait for confirmation.

Tomas said nothing.

That silence followed her across the platform toward the old mechanism. Beneath her boots, the tower’s bones shifted in the wind. Far below, the canal began to fill with the returning tide.

Mara set the first charge against the maintenance line.

The lock clicked once.

Then twice.

The third click came late, and something deep beneath Saint Orra answered with a slow iron knock.

She placed her palm against the stone and felt the tower tremble.

For one last moment, she could choose delay. She could lower the charges and return to the careful plan—the plan that left room for error, mercy, and the possibility that truth might be enough.

Then she pictured the Council’s evacuation lists, their neat columns of names and destinations. She pictured South Hook waiting behind chained gates while the elevated wards climbed toward dry ground.

Mara struck the ignition line into place.

“Ring,” she whispered.

And chose the danger that would make the whole city hear.

chapters.name: Bell Rats
chapters.content:
The market tower had once sold spices, silk, and imported glass. Its lower floors were water, and its upper galleries leaned together like exhausted buildings. A corroded sign still hung over the entrance:

**MERCY MARKET**

Mara guided the lead boat beneath it.

“Not there,” she said.

Juno studied the dark opening. “It’s the only passage.”

“The current is turning.”

“It’s water.”

“It’s turning twice.”

Pell leaned over the engine housing. “She’s right. There’s a cross-channel beneath the west wall.”

Juno gave the order. The boat angled toward a gap between buildings, where a red arrow marked the stone above the flood. Old evacuation code. **Safe depth. Controlled current.**

The paint was wet.

The passage narrowed. Both boats scraped brick. Ahead, a rope dipped almost invisibly beneath the surface.

“Stop.”

The boatman pulled the oar. Mara lifted the rope with her rod. Three tin cups had been tied along it. Water filled them, weighing the line low. A crude bell system. When the current shifted, the cups would strike the wall.

“Someone knows we’re here,” Tomas said.

“Someone wants us to know.”

Shapes moved above the market tower. Weapons rose on both boats.

“Hold,” Mara ordered.

The figures leaned over the broken railings. A woman carried a cleaver. Beside her, someone held a crossbow made from pump tubing. A child watched between them.

The woman called down, “Say it.”

“What?”

“The city.”

“Veyr.”

“Your name.”

Mara felt the guards looking at her. “Mara Venn.”

A murmur traveled through the tower.

“Bellmaker,” the woman said.

The word passed from mouth to mouth.

Tomas stepped beside Mara. “We need shelter and dry ground. We have injured people.”

“You have Council boats,” the woman replied.

“We were sent by the Council,” Juno said.

“Then drown somewhere official.”

“Open the gate,” Mara said.

The crossbow lifted.

Juno raised her pistol. Mara caught her wrist.

“Shoot and they drop the rope,” Mara said. “We lose the passage.”

“Let them drop it.”

Below them, the water clicked against submerged stone.

Mara looked up. “What do you want?”

“A reason not to kill you.”

“You can’t kill all of us.”

“No,” the woman said. “But we can kill enough.”

The cargo platform descended on chains. The first boat passed beneath. The second caught the current and swung broadside. Tomas and Juno pushed from the wall while Mara found the hidden edge of the cross-channel with her rod.

A child on the platform pointed at her. “You’re the one from the pictures.”

The woman pulled him back.

“Did you break the bells?” he asked.

Mara’s hand tightened around the rod.

The old answer rose automatically: *The Council broke the city first.*

She did not say it.

“Yes.”

The woman’s face changed. Not surprise. Recognition.

The second boat slid beneath the platform.

Inside the tower, the air smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, mold, and too many people. Stalls had been stripped into sleeping compartments. Ropes marked walkways above the open shaft. Blue lanterns gave every face the color of drowned things.

The woman waited near the winch. “I am Aven Marr. Elder of this tower.”

“Captain Juno Sarr.”

“Medic Ilya Renn.”

“Engineer Oris Pell.”

“Tomas Vale.”

Aven’s eyes rested on Mara.

Mara said nothing.

“I know who you are,” Aven said. “You may keep your name.”

Ilya climbed from the boat and took the rescued baby from its mother. The guards carried out the injured old man. The tower’s people made room, but not for Mara.

At the far end of the gallery, someone had painted a black rat with a bell around its neck.

**CONTAMINATED BELL RATS WILL BE REMOVED.**

A horn sounded outside.

Every face turned toward the broken windows. Three white lamps moved through the rain on a patrol barge.

A loudspeaker crackled. “By order of the Veyr Council, all contaminated persons are to present themselves for examination and relocation. Resistance will be treated as bell-rat insurgency.”

“The camps are dry,” the child whispered.

“They lie,” Aven said.

The speaker continued. “Salvage rights will be granted to registered households following clearance.”

Mara counted the boats and approaches. Three patrol vessels. Four defensible entrances. The eastern lane was shallow beneath the market sign. The freight crane still had power. The cargo platform could be raised. If they dropped the crane arm across the lane—

“Move the children to the north gallery,” she said. “Block the stair with grain bins. Put your strongest people on the west landing. The Council boats will come under the market sign. Cut the platform once they board.”

Aven stared at her.

“You have three minutes,” Mara said. “Perhaps less.”

“Positions,” Juno told the guards.

“No,” Aven said.

Juno turned. “What?”

“No one takes positions because the Bellmaker told them to.”

The patrol boats entered the square.

Mara pointed toward the lamps. “You can debate my reputation after they come through the windows.”

Aven stepped between her and the survivors. “You mistake fear for authority.”

“I mistake nothing. I can see the approach.”

“And I can see you.”

The words struck harder than Mara expected.

“You give orders because the room becomes unbearable when no one obeys you,” Aven said. “Your Council does the same. It calls command protection. It calls exclusion triage. It calls the people beneath its walls contaminated. You call it necessary engineering.”

Ilya looked at Mara.

The patrol horn sounded again.

Mara felt panic arrange itself into numbers: armed men, angles, load-bearing pillars, likely casualties. A plan was a door against uncertainty.

“Then make your own defense,” she said.

“We have.”

Aven lifted two fingers.

The tower came alive. A boy pulled a cord, and the blue lanterns went dark. Women at the northern windows threw powdered lime into the rain. Men hauled a net of sharpened scrap across the eastern opening. Somewhere below, a valve screamed open. Water surged through the market’s lower level, lifting abandoned carts into the patrol lane.

The first boat struck the carts and spun. Its lamps went out.

Crossbow bolts snapped from the dark.

The second boat fired blindly. A bullet punched through a pillar beside Mara, showering her with plaster. Tomas dragged her behind a stall.

“Are you hurt?”

“Don’t ask questions you know the answer to.”

Juno fired three controlled shots through the broken window. A patrolman cried out.

A handbell rang twice. The survivors shifted positions. Aven called for the north gallery to hold.

The third boat approached from the west.

Mara saw its wake strike the tower’s submerged foundation. A crack had opened along the base. The vessel’s weight would widen it. The tower would settle, then shear toward the square.

“Juno!” Mara shouted. “Get them away from the west wall!”

Aven heard. “How do you know?”

“I know towers.”

The boat struck.

The gallery lurched. People screamed. A child fell against the railing; Ilya caught him.

Mara ran to the western landing. Patrolmen were climbing from the boat.

“Cut the mooring!” she yelled. “The foundation is failing!”

“There are people below,” Aven said.

“Then move them!”

“You don’t command this tower.”

“Your tower is coming down.”

Aven searched Mara’s face, perhaps looking for the pleasure of another collapse.

Mara forced herself to breathe. Four in. Hold two. Out six.

“I need three people with axes,” she said. “The boat is wedged against the wall. If it stays, the lower supports fail. The people below have less than a minute.”

Aven released her. “Rusk. Mella. Oren. With me.”

They descended the tilted stair. Water sloshed around Mara’s knees. Three people were trapped behind a collapsed display wall: an old man, a girl, and a woman with blood on her mouth.

“Leave them,” Rusk said. “Cut the boat first.”

Mara saw the calculation form in him and recognized it.

“No,” she said. “Cut the wall. Then the mooring.”

They worked. The axe bit through wet timber. The girl screamed whenever the tower shifted. Mella dragged the old man free. The woman could not stand. Mara lifted her and carried her toward the stair.

A shot struck the water beside Mara’s foot.

Rusk threw a hook. It caught the Council boat. He and Oren hacked at the mooring line while Mella climbed with the girl.

The boat pulled away. For an instant the line held taut. Then it snapped.

The vessel swung into the square, taking two soldiers with it. The tower settled back against its foundations.

Mara reached the gallery carrying the wounded woman. Ilya took her without thanks.

The patrol boats retreated through the rain.

Aven raised the cargo platform and led Mara, Tomas, Pell, and Juno into an upper chamber that had once been a counting room. Shelves held ledgers sealed in waxed canvas, maps rolled in oilskin, and metal boxes marked with district codes.

“We found these behind the spice vault,” Aven said. “The patrols came twice for them. They called them contamination records.”

Pell opened a box. Inside were punched brass strips and folded pump diagrams. He spread one across the table.

Mara knew the pattern before she read the labels: South Hook. Kestrel. Lantern Ward. Blue arrows redirected emergency pressure away from the lower districts and toward elevated holding basins.

“Recent?” Tomas asked.

Pell examined the dates. “Three months.”

Aven placed a ledger beside the map. “We watched the pump crews. They were ordered to shut the lower intakes before each surge. Gates opened for the northern wards.”

Mara turned the pages.

Names. Times. Gate numbers. Barge manifests. Relocation quotas.

One line was stamped in red:

**BELL-RAT CLEARANCE—MARKET, SOUTH HOOK, KESTREL.**

Below it, a column listed salvageable structures.

No names of the living.

Only buildings.

Ilya stood in the doorway. Her face had gone still.

Mara slid the ledger toward her.

Ilya read the page. Her thumb stopped over Kestrel Street.

“My mother had a room above the fish ovens,” she said. “My brother was six. My father carried him to the rescue gate. Soldiers told them the hospital route had priority.”

Aven’s mouth tightened. “There was no hospital convoy.”

“I know.”

“The gate was chained from the outside,” Aven said. “We watched them do it.”

Ilya kept looking at the ledger. “They said the water was contaminated.”

“It was,” Mara said. “In some districts.”

Ilya looked up sharply.

Mara heard the mistake. A qualification placed between grief and its object.

“The Council used the warning to close the routes,” she said.

“My family was behind a gate,” Ilya replied. “They were dead because men decided an empty hospital mattered more.”

“I know.”

“No. You know the arrangement. You know the pressure and timing of the locks. You describe a death until it becomes part of a system.”

Mara looked down at the maps.

For twelve years she had carried the city as a machine: valves, towers, gates, pressure, failure. If she found the hidden mechanism, she could name the hand that turned it. If she named the hand, she would not have to remember the faces.

Aven gathered the papers.

“You will not command our people,” she said. “Tell us what the water is doing. Tell us which walls will fall. You may not decide who stands where, who remains behind, or whose life is an acceptable delay.”

The words returned to Mara from the bakery: *seventeen to twenty minutes.* She had offered the number as if it were clean, as if a child could be placed on one side of an equation and the expedition’s objective on the other.

Outside, beneath the market tower, something struck the submerged foundation.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

Everyone fell silent.

The child with the red band appeared at the doorway. “That’s the bell rats,” he whispered.

Mara looked at the black painted creature on the wall.

“No,” she said.

The third tap faded through the tower’s bones.

“They’re people,” Mara said. “They’re telling us where they are.”

chapters.name: The Night of Bells
chapters.content:
## The Night of Bells

Mara remembered the first bell as a note so clean it seemed to divide the night.

She stood beneath Saint Orra’s tower with one hand on the relay housing and the other wrapped around the copper key. Rain ran down the back of her neck. The stone beneath her boots trembled with the weight of the counterweight beginning its descent.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the bell rang.

The sound passed through her bones before it reached the air. It rose from Saint Orra in a vast bronze concussion, a single note that made the tower windows shiver and sent the pigeons bursting from the eaves. Across the river, Tower Seven answered. Then Four. Then Nine.

Veyr rang.

Mara laughed.

She could not help it. Twelve years later, she would remember the laugh more clearly than the detonation: bright, startled, almost girlish. She had imagined this moment in workshops and stolen rooms, over maps spread across dockside tables, while Nessa Quill sharpened a pencil with a knife and Tomas warned her, again and again, that warning systems were not weapons.

Now every bell in the city was speaking at once.

The concealed return line had taken the pulse exactly as she designed it. Saint Orra’s signal leapt through the old maintenance circuit, crossed the river beneath the paving stones, and woke the towers one after another. It was not a warning for one district, or an alarm limited by Council permission. It was a command the city could not ignore.

Listen, she thought.

Listen to what they have done.

The first ring rolled over the tide districts and climbed the terraces toward the elevated wards. Shutters opened. Lamps appeared in windows. People came out onto balconies and bridges, faces lifted toward the sound.

They would see the patrol routes change. They would see the reserved trains moving north. They would hear the evacuation codes that the Council had buried in their ledgers. They would understand that the flood was not an accident, not an act of weather, not a failure for which the lower districts could be blamed.

They would hear the truth.

Mara had hidden the message inside the rhythm. Three long strikes, two short, a pause, then the sequence again. Every signal engineer in Veyr knew the pattern. It meant that the ordinary channels had failed. It meant that a citywide emergency had been declared.

The bells rang it from every tower.

She pictured the streets opening. Dockworkers breaking the chains across the northern roads. Mothers carrying children through gates that had always been marked private. Council households emerging from their warm rooms to find the people they had abandoned filling the avenues.

She pictured fear changing direction.

The plan was not destruction. She knew that. She had calculated the load-bearing tolerances, the current speeds, the probable crowd movements. The charges had been placed along the relay housings, not the foundations. Saint Orra’s counterweight might drop hard, but the tower would hold. The flood channels would remain within their banks. The warning system would force the Council to act before the next surge.

A spectacle, yes. A shock. But not a massacre.

She had told herself that until the words became part of her breathing.

The bells rang louder.

At the base of Saint Orra, someone shouted her name. Perhaps Tomas. Perhaps Nessa. Perhaps a guard who had seen the flash from the service stair. Mara did not turn. She was watching the city.

Beyond the black roofs, the tide canal shone with broken reflections. The upper city glittered above it, all its windows burning gold. For the first time, Mara felt the whole of Veyr gathered inside a single mechanism, and her hand was on the lever.

She had wanted information to become power.

Now power was sound.

Then Saint Orra folded.

The memory did not move forward. It broke.

A tower of stone and iron bent toward the canal with a noise like a ship splitting open. The bell swung once, enormous and dark, and struck the collapsing frame. Its voice became a raw metallic shriek. The counterweight dropped through three floors, ripping beams and staircases loose. Masonry burst outward.

Mara remembered the tower leaning.

She remembered the canal rising to meet it.

She remembered a lamp spinning through the rain.

Afterward, she had said the charges must have been altered.

For twelve years she had said it in different forms. The Council had sabotaged the relay. A hidden explosive had been planted beneath Saint Orra. The tower’s old foundations had already been compromised by deliberate neglect. All of those things could be true. Some of them were true.

But her hand had turned the key.

The canal swallowed the lower half of Saint Orra. Its foundations struck the retaining wall and punched through it. Water erupted into the maintenance quarter, carrying masonry, cables, carts, and people. The first surge ran west toward the chemical stores.

Mara had not known the reservoir gates were chained open.

Or perhaps she had known they were old and unreliable and decided that knowledge was not the same as responsibility.

The memory changed again.

A tower bell rang.

A second bell answered.

Then something beneath the city gave way.

The chemical reservoir ruptured with a sound too small for the destruction that followed. A seam opened in the tank wall, and yellow water spread across the lower street. It met the canal surge at the corner of Fallow Lane. The two currents rolled together, bright with oil and industrial dye.

People ran into it.

Some fell immediately. Others stumbled on, blinded and coughing, their skin shining under the alarm lamps. The rain struck the poisoned water and lifted a bitter vapor that coated Mara’s tongue.

She remembered thinking: The wind will carry it north.

Then she remembered the wind had changed.

There were always calculations. There was always one more current, one more pressure, one more gate whose condition had not been included in the model. She had believed a city could be made to behave if she understood enough of its parts.

But Veyr was not a diagram.

It was stone and weather and frightened bodies. It was old repairs laid over older failures. It was a Council that had designed every system to protect someone else first.

It was a child pounding on a shelter gate.

Mara heard the pounding now.

Not in the street. Not through the rain. Somewhere behind the walls of memory, fists struck iron in a frantic, uneven rhythm.

Open!

The shelter at Kestrel Street had been built beneath the transit embankment. Its gates were supposed to release automatically when the warning network declared a flood emergency. Mara had inspected the mechanism twice. She knew the power relay, the manual override, the pressure door.

She remembered reaching the control station.

She remembered the gate lamps burning red.

She remembered pulling the lever and finding no response.

The official account said Council troops sealed the shelter to prevent panic. The records would later show that the gates had been locked from outside. Mara had repeated this to herself until it became proof of everything she believed.

But another image forced itself through.

The relay panel beneath her hand, sparks spitting from the cracked housing.

Her own signal had overloaded the district circuit.

The shelter lights had gone dark after Saint Orra fell.

Behind the gates, people screamed.

Mara had run along the service corridor searching for the secondary release. She had shouted that she was trying to open it. She had promised she could fix the system.

The pounding had continued.

She had been close enough to touch the gate.

There had been a child’s voice among the others, high and hoarse from calling for her mother.

Mara had not known the child’s name. She still did not.

The memory withdrew before she could hear how the voice ended.

Instead, she saw the barricades.

The northern avenue was packed with people carrying bundles, children, tools, cages, anything they had managed to seize before the water reached their homes. They had heard the bells and believed the routes were open. They surged toward the elevated wards, toward the rail platforms whose lamps shone above the flood.

At the avenue mouth, Council soldiers had built a barricade from wagons and iron fencing.

Behind it, the road was empty.

Mara remembered this as evidence. She remembered the obscene emptiness of the reserved route, the way the soldiers stood beneath dry awnings while lower-district families pushed against the barriers. She remembered thinking that if the people could see this, the Council would fall by morning.

The crowd pushed.

The soldiers lowered their weapons.

Someone threw a stone.

Then the barricade moved—not toward the crowd, but inward, its wheels rolling as the soldiers dragged it shut across the avenue.

The people behind it screamed.

The people ahead of it screamed louder.

Water poured through the side streets and trapped them between the fencing and the embankment. A woman lifted a baby over her head. A man tried to climb the ironwork and was struck down by a rifle butt. The crowd became a single heaving animal, every body pressed against the next, unable to advance or retreat.

Mara had believed the barricades were the Council’s choice.

They were.

She had also believed the bells would make the choice visible without making the crowd desperate enough to break itself against it.

That had been her choice too.

The warning pulse raced beyond the towers. It entered the old maintenance lines, crossed circuits that had not been tested in decades, and triggered emergency releases in districts where the channels were already under pressure. Gates opened where they should have remained closed. Others sealed against the surge. Pumps reversed. Reservoirs filled.

The flood did not move like an army obeying a command.

It moved like a chain of doors thrown open in darkness.

One district drowned another.

At South Hook, a pressure gate tore from its hinges and struck the pump housing. At Lantern Ward, a drainage tunnel collapsed under the weight of a diverted channel. At the old glassworks, fire rolled across the surface of the water when the oil stores overturned.

All of it began with the bells.

No—that was not right.

All of it began before the bells, in decisions made by men who had never walked the lower streets. In walls left thin, pumps moved north, emergency routes reserved for the people who could afford to be counted. The city had been arranged as a trap long before Mara touched the key.

But the bells sprung it.

She remembered the exhilaration because it had been real.

For the first seconds, perhaps the first minute, she had believed herself victorious. She stood beneath the rain while the towers spoke, and every sound seemed to confirm her judgment. The city was awake. The Council was exposed. The poor were no longer invisible.

Then the bells began to fall silent.

One by one, the towers stopped answering.

Four went quiet after its upper platform collapsed into the tramway. Nine continued ringing without rhythm, its mechanism locked in a damaged cycle. Tower Seven gave a final concussion that shattered windows for three streets around, and then the sound disappeared beneath the roar of water.

Saint Orra’s bell was still moving when Mara saw the canal take the first houses.

Their roofs surfaced briefly, lamps glowing in attic windows. People waved from the upper floors. The flood reached them before any rescue boat could turn against the current.

She tried to tell herself that the Council had caused this.

It had.

She tried to tell herself that the city would remember why.

It did not matter.

A hand caught her sleeve. Tomas stood beside her, soaked through, blood running from his temple. His mouth formed words she could not hear.

The bells were too loud.

Or perhaps they were already gone, and the silence in her ears had begun.

He pointed toward the canal. Then toward the eastern service road. Then at Mara herself.

She understood him anyway.

What have you done?

She wanted to answer that she had made them listen. She wanted to tell him that history would not remember the quiet compromises, the delayed repairs, the sealed ledgers. It would remember the night the bells rang together and Veyr was forced to see its own design.

But behind Tomas, the crowd at Kestrel Street was still pounding on the gate.

The sound traveled through the rain.

Three strikes. A pause. Three more.

Mara looked toward the shelter.

The street had become a river. Bodies moved in it, some walking, some carried, some already still. The red gate lamps flickered above the water. She could not see the people behind the doors, but she knew they were there. She knew they had heard the bells and believed someone had finally come to open the way.

Her hand was still wrapped around the copper key.

She let go.

The next wave struck the embankment and rose higher than the lamps.

Tomas pulled her back as the service road vanished beneath it. Mara stumbled, fought him for one furious instant, and then followed him into the tunnels while the city drowned above them.

Behind her, Veyr’s bells rang without mercy.

Ahead, in the dark, people screamed her name.

chapters.name: Poison Water
chapters.content:
The water beyond Mercy Market changed color at the third bellpost.

Until then it had been the ordinary gray-brown of a drowned city, carrying roof tiles, dead weeds, splintered doors, and shapes Mara refused to identify. At the bellpost, violet slid beneath a skin of yellow. Green fumes trembled over the surface, gathering in the lee of the buildings.

Oris Pell lifted his instrument.

“Don’t,” Mara said.

He stopped with the glass probe suspended above the water. “I’m not touching it.”

“You’re breathing it.”

He coughed once. Ilya Renn snapped, “Mask.”

Oris fumbled with the respirator at his neck. The buckle slipped twice before he secured it. His gloves were stiff with salt and old oil, and his fingers shook—not from fear, Mara thought, but from the cold.

“Your hands,” she said.

“Are attached.”

“Barely useful, then.”

Ilya gave Mara a flat look. “You could try concern.”

“Concern does not improve dexterity.”

“Neither does being drowned.”

Juno Sarr raised a hand. The expedition halted on the upper floor of a drowned countinghouse. Below, six feet of chemical water filled the street. A tram cable sagged between buildings, its copper strands shining like wet hair. Across the way, a painted sign for a cooper’s guild showed through the haze, its letters blistered and running.

The fumes came from somewhere ahead.

Mara crouched beside the broken floor and watched the current. The violet water did not spread evenly. It separated around submerged foundations, then joined again beneath the leaning warehouses. A second current moved below the first, visible only when scraps of paper dipped and vanished.

“Old reservoir,” she said. “Glassworks or dye houses.”

“Both are west,” Oris replied. He drew a damp chart from inside his coat and held it against the wall. “The pressure maps show the reservoirs were emptied after the first flood.”

“The maps are wrong.”

“Most maps are wrong when you’re standing in them.”

He tried to make it a joke. No one smiled.

Mara pointed to the water. “See the surface tension near the bellpost? It’s drawing toward the old drainage spine. The reservoir is not empty. It’s leaking through a buried wall.”

Oris leaned closer. “If the lower channel is open, the western roofs may still be accessible. We could cross above the contamination and reach the archive tower.”

“You see poison and call it a passage.”

“I see a current. I need a reading.”

“You need to remain alive.”

“I’m the only one here who can interpret the result.”

Mara stepped between him and the opening. “Find it from here.”

His expression tightened. “That isn’t a measurement.”

“It’s experience.”

“You have twelve years of experience in a cell.”

“And before that, I designed half the warning network you’re standing over.”

“The half that killed people?”

The countinghouse went silent except for the distant creak of timber. Oris seemed to regret the words as soon as they left him, but he did not withdraw them.

Mara felt the old pressure behind her ribs: anger arranging itself into clean compartments. Insult. Fear. Provocation. A choice.

She counted four breaths.

Juno glanced between them. “We’re wasting air.”

Mara turned to the boatmen. “Rope across the roofline. Tie to the chimney, then the archive tower. No one touches the water. Pell, stay behind me.”

Oris opened his mouth.

“Stay behind me,” she repeated.

Aven Marr’s younger companion, Sile, stared toward the fumes. “The tower foundation is cracked.”

“So is everything else.”

They crossed the countinghouse roof over slick tiles and rotten beams. Rain ticked against the helmets of the guards. The rope dragged behind them, dark with floodwater. Somewhere beneath the building, something struck masonry with a slow, heavy pulse.

At the midpoint, Mara stopped.

“Why?” Juno whispered.

She pointed to the chimney.

A thin line of bubbles rose beside it. Not bubbles from a leak. Air pushed upward through a submerged vent, carrying a sharp almond smell.

“Reservoir gas,” she said. “Keep low.”

The group lowered themselves. They moved on hands and knees until the wind shifted and carried the vapor away. Oris began to cough behind his mask.

Mara looked back. “Pell.”

“I’m fine.”

“You are not.”

“I’m conscious.”

“That is a temporary condition.”

They reached the chimney. Mara looped the rope twice around its base and tested the mortar with her boot. The chimney shifted.

“Not here,” she said. “Sile, find another anchor.”

Sile crossed toward the tower. Three steps from the chimney, the roof gave way.

Oris vanished.

He struck the water below. The rope jerked. Juno caught it and threw himself backward, boots skidding over the tiles, while Sile seized the line beside him.

“Don’t pull!” Oris shouted.

His voice came from beneath the surface, distorted by water.

The rope continued to run.

Mara seized it. The current moved with him. She saw his harness caught below, the brass instrument case twisting beside his shoulder.

“Cut him loose,” Juno said.

Mara looked down.

The water was perhaps twelve feet deep. If the harness had snagged on a beam, pulling might free him. If the case had caught him, the rope would drag him under. The meter was irreplaceable. Oris was not.

His lungs were already filling.

“Cut the case,” she said.

Juno drew his knife.

“Not the rope.”

The line surged. Oris broke the surface, gasped, and disappeared.

Mara saw his hand.

She went in.

The water closed above her head, cold and burning. Chemical sting pierced her gloves and slid beneath her collar. Her mask filled with violet murk. She found Oris below, one boot wedged between beams, eyes wide behind his lenses.

He had lost his respirator.

Bubbles tore from his mouth.

Mara reached for his foot. The current shoved them sideways. Her shoulder struck a support. Pain flashed down her arm. Oris fought her, panicking, his hands clawing at the beam and at her face.

She caught his wrist and pinned it against his chest.

Count.

Locate the obstruction.

Free the foot.

Turn him toward the surface.

The water was not the tower. It was not Saint Orra. It did not answer to a rhythm or obey a diagram. It had no center, no command point, no single failure she could correct.

Oris kicked wildly. His other boot struck her knee.

Mara found the trapped foot and drove her elbow against the beam. Once. Twice. The timber groaned. On the third blow, the leather tore and his foot came free.

His instrument case remained caught.

Its strap snagged Mara’s wrist.

For one instant the world became weight, pressure, and choice. She drew her knife and cut the strap.

The case disappeared into the dark.

The loss pulled at her more sharply than she expected. Instruments could be replaced, but not in the undercity. Without Oris’s calibrations, they might reach the engine blind. Without Oris, they might never reach it at all.

She wrapped an arm around his chest and kicked upward. He had gone slack. Her lungs convulsed. Above them, daylight wavered through the broken roof, shattered into green and yellow bands.

She shoved him toward the light and followed.

Juno and Sile hauled Oris onto the tiles. Ilya dragged Mara after him by the back of her coat. Mara rolled onto her side and vomited yellow water. Her throat felt flayed.

Ilya was already checking Oris’s throat. “No pulse.”

Juno began compressions.

“His left leg was caught,” Mara said. “He aspirated. His mask was lost at—”

“Could you stop talking?”

“He was under less than a minute.”

“Let me work.”

“He may have inhaled reservoir solvent.”

“Let me work.”

Juno counted compressions, each number forced through clenched teeth. Rain ran from his helmet onto Oris’s face.

Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen.

Mara crawled away from them and stripped off her gloves. The skin beneath was blotched crimson. She examined each finger, flexed the joints, and found them functional.

At thirty, Ilya breathed into Oris’s mouth.

At sixty, Juno’s arms shook.

At ninety, Oris convulsed and expelled yellow water. He coughed until blood spotted his lips.

Ilya rolled him onto his side. “Again. Breathe. Slowly. Don’t fight the cough.”

Oris’s eyes opened. He gripped her sleeve.

Juno sat back, breathing hard.

“You went in after him,” he said.

Mara wiped her mouth with the heel of her hand. “His death would have delayed the crossing.”

“You cut loose the instruments.”

“After they became a liability.”

“The case contained the only working pressure meter.”

“It was pulling him down.”

“You could have lost both.”

“I didn’t.”

Ilya looked at her with open hatred. “Could you make one human statement?”

Mara looked at Oris. He was shivering beneath the rain, his face gray, his bare foot bleeding through the torn boot.

“That was one.”

“It was a measurement.”

Mara turned toward the archive tower.

Its foundation had not failed entirely. A stone buttress leaned against the warehouse, and behind it an iron door showed above the waterline. The lock was new. Its polished surface had not been touched by the flood.

“Inside,” Mara said.

Juno rose. “We’re not moving until Pell can stand.”

“Then we shelter here.”

They carried Oris across the roof. The archive door opened onto a dry passage sloping beneath the tower. He was supported between Juno and Sile, one arm over each shoulder. Ilya stayed beside him, forcing him to breathe slowly and watching the color of his lips.

The passage ended at a brick wall. New mortar outlined one section. Mara scraped it away with a pry bar and found a steel hatch painted Council gray.

Tomas Vale stopped behind her.

“That mark,” he said.

A black square had been stamped into the steel. Beneath it, nearly erased, were the words CIVIC CONTINUANCE—AUTHORIZED ACCESS.

“You know it?” Juno asked.

“I know the classification.”

“Meaning?”

“Emergency reserves. Restricted distribution. Usually attached to evacuation infrastructure.”

Mara turned the release wheel. It opened easily.

The room beyond was sealed, dry, and cold. Shelves lined every wall. Crates filled the center. A lantern hung from the ceiling, its oil still clear. No dust lay on the desk.

Someone had used the room recently.

The first crate held purification tablets. The second held bandages, filters, and dried food. The third held stamped metal tags.

Ilya lifted one.

“Relocation,” she read. “South Hook Sector. Labor intake.”

Her voice changed on the last words.

Mara opened a ledger on the desk.

Households assessed. Structures claimed. Workers assigned. Transport priority.

Below the headings, the same instructions appeared:

SURVIVORS TO BE REGISTERED BEFORE ASSISTANCE.

UNREGISTERED PERSONS SUBJECT TO TRANSFER.

MUNICIPAL LABOR REQUIREMENT: THREE YEARS.

At the bottom, in red ink:

CLEARANCE TO BEGIN AFTER NEXT SURGE.

Ilya’s face hardened. “Relocation camps.”

“Labor camps,” Tomas said.

She looked at him. “Tell that to the people inside them.”

He did not answer.

Mara opened another folder. Maps of the undercity were marked in red: South Hook, Kestrel, Lantern Ward, Mercy Market. Lines led north toward elevated rail stations and industrial compounds. Each route ended in a box labeled INTAKE.

Not shelter. Not hospital.

Intake.

Oris pushed himself upright against the wall. “The current wasn’t accidental,” he said. His voice was raw, but steadier. “They opened the lower channels to drive survivors toward those routes.”

“Or drive them away from the redevelopment zones,” Juno said.

Mara studied the maps. “Both.”

Aven’s records had shown redirection from the lower basins. These maps showed where the people would go afterward. The Council had not merely failed to save them. It had prepared to count them, claim them, and work them.

Tomas lifted a thin folder and turned it over without opening it.

“The Council used the same language after the Night of Bells,” he said.

Mara looked at him.

“Temporary registration. Industrial reassignment. Emergency custody.”

“You were there.”

“I read the records.”

“You investigated them.”

“Not then.”

“You knew.”

His thumb pressed into the folder’s edge. “I knew pieces.”

“Pieces become a structure when enough people refuse to name it.”

“I was trying to find proof.”

“You were trying to survive.”

His eyes met hers. “Both.”

The lantern hissed. Water pressed against the walls. In the cramped room, Oris’s breathing and the drip from Mara’s coat sounded like two competing clocks.

Mara placed her palm on the ledger. “Say what you mean.”

Tomas looked at the names: hundreds of households reduced to columns, the living sorted by usefulness.

“The official account said your signal caused the collapse, the chemical release, the gate failures, the crowd deaths. It said the Council responded to an unforeseen catastrophe.”

“And?”

“The response plans existed before the towers fell.”

“That does not absolve me.”

“I didn’t say it did.”

“You’re beginning to.”

“The city was already arranged for disaster. Perhaps not the exact disaster, perhaps not the way it happened. But the sealed gates, reserved trains, and labor routes existed before Saint Orra rang.”

Mara’s fingers tightened on the paper until the page creased.

She remembered Northern Avenue: the barricades, the crowd surging toward an empty route, the water rising behind them. She had driven them there with her impossible alarm. The Council had built the fence and posted soldiers before the first bell.

Both things could be true.

No division of blame returned a single body to the living.

Tomas lowered his voice. “The Night of Bells was not one act.”

Mara looked at the hatch, the labor ledgers, and Oris breathing shallowly while Ilya checked his pupils.

“No,” she said. “It was a system.”

For once, Tomas did not argue.

From beneath the floor came three dull knocks.

Mara turned toward the sound.

Three taps. A pause.

Then three more.

The lantern flame bent toward the bricks, as if the sealed room itself had drawn breath.

chapters.name: After the Ringing
chapters.content:
The third knock beneath the archive floor did not sound like a hand.

It sounded like a tool striking a pipe far below, a dull metal note traveling through brick and water. Mara held her breath. The lantern flame leaned toward the mortar.

Three strikes.

A pause.

Three more.

The rhythm entered her like a key, and the door she had kept shut for twelve years opened.

She was back in the city.

The first thing she remembered was rain rising from the ground. It burst through grates, poured from stairwells, and carried lamp oil, ash, sewage, dye, and the sharp stink of the sea.

Mara stood waist-deep beneath the eastern rail bridge, one hand gripping a rusted ladder, the other pressed to her mouth.

“Again!” someone shouted.

Three workers leaned against a gate wheel inside the tunnel. Ropes crossed their shoulders. Each time they pulled, the wheel turned a fraction, then shuddered back. Behind the gate, people pounded the iron.

“Cut the lock!” Mara called.

“We tried!”

“Use the thermal saw.”

“It drowned.”

“Then use a charge.”

The worker nearest her stared. “There are people on the other side.”

“I know.”

“If we break it—”

“Break it carefully.”

He shouted for the saw. Mara moved along the platform, counting the intervals between surges. Seven seconds. Six. Eight. The flood was not random. Somewhere beneath the city, pumps were opening and closing in a pattern no one had designed for a living city.

A woman clung to a bridge support. “My boy went through the east shelter!”

“What shelter?”

“Kestrel Street. They said the doors were open. They said the northern route—”

A wave struck the bridge. Mara caught the woman’s coat before she vanished.

“Kestrel is sealed,” Mara said.

The woman’s face changed.

Behind them, the pounding became a roar. The thermal saw sparked once and died. One worker attacked the lock housing with a hammer while another climbed onto the wheel.

“Back!” Mara shouted.

The gate bulged inward.

A crack split the air.

The workers released the wheel. The gate burst. A black wall of water filled the tunnel, lifting men from their feet and flinging them against the bridge. Mara struck a pillar and felt something break in her shoulder.

When she surfaced, the water had reached her throat.

The city was ringing.

Saint Orra sounded first, vast and triumphant. Tower Seven answered from the west, then Four, then Nine. The notes collided over the rooftops. Mara laughed with blood in her mouth. The warning worked. The hidden evacuation pattern was no longer hidden. Veyr would see which routes opened and which stayed barred.

Then Saint Orra gave a grinding shriek.

The counterweight struck its housing. The retaining wall below the tower failed.

The water changed direction.

Afterward, no one agreed what had happened first. The chemical reservoir ruptured before the southern pumps reversed, or the pumps reversed because the reservoir had ruptured. The tower fell into the canal, or the canal rose to swallow it. Kestrel’s shelter gate sealed before the relay burned, or the relay burned when Mara’s signal overloaded the controls.

There had been too many systems and too little truth.

She remembered fragments.

A man carrying a child whose hair was white with chemical foam.

A woman searching beneath a fallen beam for a wedding ring.

Workers crawling across the roof of Kestrel shelter while people inside pounded the gates.

A line of soldiers on Northern Avenue, rifles leveled at the flood.

“Turn back!” one shouted.

The crowd did not. Mara’s warning had sent them toward the route she believed would open. The Council had barricaded it hours before.

The soldiers fired above their heads first.

Then into the crowd.

Mara did not see the second volley. She heard it while running through a flooded lane. Later she learned that people had been shot, trampled, or drowned between the rails. The list made no distinctions.

The Council did.

By afternoon, loudspeakers had been mounted on the intact towers.

“Citizens of Veyr,” a calm voice announced, “the terrorist Mara Venn and her Bellmaker cell have attacked the warning network. Their deliberate act has caused the deaths of thousands.”

The voice belonged to Councilor Halvek, though Mara did not know that then.

“Do not approach members of the resistance. Do not shelter accomplices. The state will restore order.”

The state restored order by sealing the lower bridges.

Mara found Nessa near the old tram depot, kneeling beside bodies. She recognized Nessa’s coat before her face. One shoulder was burned, and her hands were red to the wrists.

“Lio?” Mara asked.

Nessa pointed toward the depot entrance.

The bodies lay beneath tarps. One wore a signalman’s jacket. Another had a dockworker’s blue scarf. The third was too small to belong to the crew, and Mara refused to ask why.

She pulled back the jacket.

Lio’s eyes were closed. A cut crossed his cheek. He looked younger than he had that morning, when he had asked whether Saint Orra could really be made to ring with the other towers.

Nessa spoke behind her. “He was at Tower Four. The charge went early.”

“It was timed.”

“It went early.”

Mara looked toward the street. Water carried splinters and paper past the depot.

“Where are Vey and the others?”

“Some ran. Some were taken.”

“Taken where?”

Nessa gave a humorless laugh. “You still think there is a where.”

A crowd had gathered at the end of the street, carrying pipes and broken boards. Someone had painted a bell on the depot wall, then crossed it out.

“They’re coming,” Nessa said.

“They’re looking for Council informants.”

“They’re looking for someone who did this.”

A stone struck the wall. Someone shouted, “Bellmaker!”

Mara pried open Lio’s fingers. He held a blackened brass key.

“If they catch you,” Nessa said, “they’ll tear you apart.”

“They should hear what happened.”

“They don’t want to hear. The Council has a voice on every tower.”

Another stone came through the doorway. Nessa shoved Mara toward the rear passage.

Mara hesitated, looking down at Lio.

Then she ran.

She moved through alleys filled with overturned carts and floating bodies. At the mouth of Dyer’s Lane, a woman recognized her. Disbelief became rage.

“You,” the woman said.

She held a child’s red shoe.

Mara stopped.

“You rang them.”

Mara had an answer ready—They lied to you. I exposed them. The gates were already closed—but it would not come.

The woman struck her.

Mara tasted blood.

“You rang them,” the woman said again.

Mara walked on.

By nightfall, the Council had erased the evacuation orders. It erased the maintenance notices, diverted pumps, reserved rail schedules, hospital routes, and the districts marked expendable. Every broadcast repeated the same account: Mara Venn had designed the attack, selected the targets, and ordered the towers to ring. She had intended to drown the lower city because ordinary citizens opposed liberation.

The lie was shaped around the truth until the truth could not breathe.

Mara hid in a pump station beneath Lantern Ward. Seven recruits gathered there, two wounded and one unable to use his right hand. A cracked radio whispered:

“—sole architect—”

“—murder of families—”

“—Bellmaker terrorist network—”

Tavin threw it against the wall.

“We should surrender,” one worker said.

“They’ll kill us,” said another.

“They’re killing us already.”

Mara stood apart, soaked and shivering. Her shoulder throbbed. She could still smell the chemicals.

Nessa approached with a strip of cloth. “You’re bleeding.”

“It’s not serious.”

“I didn’t ask.”

Mara let her bind the wound.

“Did you know the lock was unstable?” Nessa asked.

The room went quiet.

“I knew there was a risk.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“Tomas inspected the chamber.”

“And?”

“He wanted more time.”

“You altered the charges.”

“To synchronize the towers.”

“You altered them.”

Mara looked at the broken radio. “If Saint Orra rang alone, they could call it a malfunction. If all four rang, the city would see the pattern.”

“The city saw you.”

Nessa turned away.

Later, Tomas found Mara in the lower access tunnel. He carried a lantern and a pistol. Blood marked his collar.

“You left the station,” he said.

“They’re searching it.”

“They already did.”

His eyes went to her bandage. “I told you the lock was unstable.”

“You said the housing was old.”

“I said the counterweight would shear if the signal load reached the upper relay.”

“You said you needed to verify the design.”

“I said delay the operation.”

“There was no delay. The Council would have moved the evacuation trains.”

“There could have been another way.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know I warned you.”

The tunnel walls trembled as water moved behind them.

“People are dying because the Council built a trap,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“Because they sealed the gates.”

“Yes.”

“Because they shot the crowd.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you looking at me as if I did this alone?”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m looking at you because you did something.”

The lantern shook between them.

Tomas lowered the pistol. “You don’t get to disappear into their lie because it contains you.”

“They’ll make me the whole disaster.”

“They will.”

“And you’ll help them?”

“I don’t know.”

That uncertainty was worse than accusation.

Voices sounded in the upper passage. Metal struck metal.

“We have to go,” Tomas said.

Mara looked at him—the man who had warned her, followed her, trusted her, and now stood between her and the dark.

“What happens if I stay?”

“They arrest you.”

“And if I run?”

“They hunt you.”

Above them, one tower began to ring. The note was cracked and uneven. It sounded once, then again, then a third time.

Mara thought of Lio beneath the jacket. The people at Kestrel. The woman with the red shoe. Every face the city would place beneath her name.

Tomas reached for her.

She stepped back.

The tunnel water surged around her boots. Mara found the maintenance ladder and descended before he could catch her.

He called her name once.

She did not answer.

Below, the flooded dark closed over her head. She swam toward the old channels, counting strokes until the bells became vibration. At the first junction she chose the passage no map recorded. At the second she killed the lantern.

In the darkness, something struck the brick.

Three times.

A pause.

Three more.

Mara pressed her palm to the wall. For an instant she imagined that the city was waiting for her answer, that some mechanism remained which she could master if she understood its rhythm.

Then she withdrew her hand and went deeper, carrying the brass key, the blood, and the knowledge that the door behind her would never open again.

chapters.name: The Records Room
chapters.content:
The three knocks came again from beneath the archive floor.

Three. A pause. Three.

Dust sifted from the beams. The lantern flame leaned toward the bricks.

Mara raised one hand. Juno stopped with her pistol half-drawn. Ilya gripped her medical satchel, while Pell, pale from the chemical poisoning, stared at the floor.

“Not a bell,” he whispered.

“A signal,” Mara said.

Tomas stood at the central desk, reading the red-marked relocation orders. He folded the page once. “We should leave.”

“Why?”

“Because whoever is below knows we’re here.”

“So does the Council.”

“And the patrols outside know where we went.”

Mara crouched and pressed her palm to the tiles. One square near the foundation held a faint warmth, a vibration against her skin. The archive had no stair, hatch, or service entrance. It had been built to be reached by someone who knew the mechanism.

She drew Lio’s brass key from beneath her collar.

Tomas saw it. His expression shifted.

“Where did you get that?”

“You know what it opens?”

“I know where it came from.”

“Then answer me.”

“It was issued to tower maintenance crews.”

“Lio carried it.”

Tomas looked at the floor. “Mara.”

She fitted the key into a seam between two tiles. It turned. The tiles sank and slid aside, revealing a square of black water. A ladder descended through it. The upper rungs were clean.

Juno came to her shoulder. “That goes down?”

“It goes somewhere.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“Guardrails rarely are.”

“Route authority isn’t command of my judgment.”

Mara lowered the lantern. The light showed a landing twenty feet below and a passage beyond it.

“Pell stays here,” Ilya said.

“I can hear you,” Pell muttered.

“Good. Hear this too: if you fall into another reservoir, I’ll let the water keep you.”

Mara descended first. The ladder ended in a tiled corridor, with water whispering beneath a metal grating. Faded arrows marked the walls. Red lamps hung in cages, though only one still burned. The air grew warmer near the pumpworks.

Tomas followed. His boots struck the grating in a rhythm she knew from another life.

“You altered the old records,” she said.

“I didn’t.”

“Not these. The tower records.”

He said nothing.

The corridor opened onto a gallery above the abandoned pumpworks. Huge cylindrical housings rose from the dark, filmed with salt. Water churned between them. At the far end stood a glass-fronted records room.

Mara approached the door.

“Wait,” Tomas said.

He pointed to a brass plaque listing the original safety releases. Four new bolts held it to the railing, while the old holes remained around them.

“Someone moved it,” Mara said.

“After the Night of Bells.”

“Why?”

“To make the system appear older than it was.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

She used the key. The records-room door opened.

Dust covered the cabinets but not the central desk. A dead lantern and a sealed metal box rested there. Mara opened the box and spread its maps across the desk.

The first showed Veyr before the disaster: tide barriers, flood channels, pumping stations, and the elevated districts marked in blue. The second showed the same network afterward.

A seawall along South Hook had been shortened by three hundred yards. The Kestrel intakes were marked nonessential. A relief channel from Lantern Ward had vanished.

Tomas leaned over the maps. “Not removed. Reassigned.”

The margins held notes in a clerk’s hand.

PRESSURE REDIRECTED TO NORTHERN BASINS.

SOUTHERN LOSS ACCEPTABLE UNDER EMERGENCY MODEL.

EVACUATION PRIORITY: REGISTERED HOUSEHOLDS, HOSPITAL PERSONNEL, INDUSTRIAL ADMINISTRATION.

Mara found a ledger beneath the maps. It listed trains, hospital beds, and transport routes. Beside the date of the Night of Bells, written in red, was:

NORTHERN TRANSFER COMPLETE AT 19:40.

The first tower had rung at 19:43.

“They were already gone,” Mara said.

“Some of them.”

“They were already gone while people in Kestrel broke shelter doors with their hands.”

Tomas did not answer.

Another ledger recorded rescue allocations. The old tram depot: three boats, crossed out. Mercy Market: none. Lantern Ward: one barge, diverted north. At the bottom was a signature.

H. HALVEK.

Juno swore under her breath.

Ilya read over Mara’s arm. Her face hardened. “So that proves it.”

“It proves they planned unequal rescue,” Tomas said.

“It proves they decided who could drown.”

“It proves part of what they decided.”

Ilya looked at him. “You speak as if the dead require footnotes.”

“I speak as if the living will use one truth to bury another.”

Mara turned. “There it is.”

“What?”

“The defense you’ve carried for twelve years. The Council lied, so no record can be trusted. The Council murdered, so my guilt becomes an administrative detail.”

“I said nothing of the kind.”

“You don’t have to.”

She shoved the ledger toward him. “You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“You knew enough to testify.”

“I knew the Council had evacuation lists. I didn’t know how much of the infrastructure was designed around them.”

“You knew enough to let them put my face on every wall.”

His eyes moved toward the churning pumps. “I knew what I could prove.”

“And what did you prove?”

“That you changed the charges.”

The words struck with the force of a dropped tool.

Mara stepped back. “You altered the maintenance records.”

“I corrected them.”

“You erased the warning.”

“I moved it.”

“You removed the note that Saint Orra’s counterweight was unstable.”

“I moved it to a restricted appendix.”

“Where no prosecutor saw it.”

“Where no prosecutor was permitted to see it.”

She laughed once. “You want that distinction to save you?”

“No.”

“You let them say the towers were sound.”

“I let them say the charges had been placed illegally.”

“They were placed illegally.”

“You knew the lock was unstable.”

“So did you.”

“I knew enough to warn you. I didn’t know the thermal failure would shear the gate, or that the relay housing would collapse, or that the Council had sealed Northern Avenue and diverted the pumps.”

“But you knew.”

“Yes.”

The pumpworks shuddered below them.

Tomas braced his hands on the desk. “After the flood, Halvek’s people found me before I reached the lower wards. They had Nessa’s name. They had lists of everyone who worked with us. They said that if I contradicted the official account, the remaining cells would be prosecuted as a conspiracy. They promised to release the maintenance crews if I signed.”

“Did they?”

“No.”

“Then you knew what their promises were worth.”

“I knew what they could do.”

“You were afraid.”

“Yes.”

The admission unsettled her more than denial would have.

“Of them. Of prison. Of what would happen if the city learned we had been warned and proceeded anyway. I told myself that keeping the records alive was more important than exposing everything. I told myself reform needed a surviving witness. I told myself your trial would leave a crack open.”

“You told yourself whatever let you sleep.”

“I didn’t sleep.”

“Then you had the privilege of being awake.”

He flinched.

She had wanted to hurt him. The satisfaction was immediate and thin.

“You let them make me a monster,” she said. “Not because you believed I was innocent. Because you thought the city could only look at one crime at a time.”

“I thought if I revealed everything, they would say the Council’s crimes excused ours.”

“They would have said that anyway.”

“Yes.”

“And you still chose silence.”

“Yes.”

For a moment, the only sound was water striking the pump housings.

Tomas opened a cabinet and removed a thin folder. “This is current.”

Inside were transfer orders dated three weeks earlier. South Hook, Kestrel, Lantern Ward, Mercy Market. The language was cleaner than the old ledgers.

CONTROLLED INUNDATION.

TEMPORARY DISPLACEMENT.

LABOR INTAKE UPON REGISTRATION.

Beside each district, a pressure figure had been written. The northern basins were marked PROTECTED. The lower districts were marked SACRIFICIAL.

“Sacrificial,” Ilya said.

“An engineer’s word,” Pell called from the entrance. He had followed them, leaning on Juno. “They use it when they want a person to sound like a component.”

Mara turned the page. A maintenance appendix had been copied after the disaster. At the bottom, in Tomas’s handwriting, was a note:

COUNTERWEIGHT INSTABILITY VERIFIED. WARNING GIVEN TO M. VENN. OPERATION PROCEEDED WITHOUT DELAY.

She stared at it.

“You kept that.”

“I kept everything I could.”

“Hidden.”

“Yes.”

“Why show me now?”

“Because you’re going to the engine.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

She folded the current orders and the appendix into her coat.

Juno stepped forward. “Those records belong to the expedition.”

“They belong to whoever can keep them from becoming ash.”

“That isn’t permission.”

“No. It’s evidence.”

Three knocks sounded beneath the floor. A pause. Three more.

Tomas moved toward the opening. “We should answer.”

“We don’t know what’s below.”

“We know they have access to the pumpworks.”

“And they may know exactly what we want.”

“Then we ask.”

“You always mistook an invitation for consent.”

His expression sharpened. “You always mistook uncertainty for a command to act.”

The words carried her back beneath Saint Orra, hearing his warning through the relay hiss.

Delay. Verify the housing. Wait.

She had heard fear and called it betrayal. She had heard the city pounding at its gates and decided only she could answer.

Mara looked at the documents in her coat. The Council had built a machine that required victims. She had seized its controls believing she could force it to confess. She had not escaped its logic. She had only taken hold of the lever.

“Get Pell upstairs,” she said.

Tomas remained by the opening. “And the people below?”

“We return with rope, light, and a route that won’t flood if the pumps cycle.”

“That sounds like delay.”

“It is.”

“You hated delay.”

“I hated not choosing it.”

The tapping stopped.

From deep beneath the pumpworks, a bell rang once. Not the city’s warning peal, but a single submerged note that traveled through the pipes and into Mara’s bones.

She closed her fist around Lio’s key.

“Now we know they’re listening,” she said.

Tomas looked at her across the records room. “No. Now they know we are.”

Mara turned toward the ladder.

Above, the archive waited with its false supplies and red clearance order. Below, the dark held whoever had learned to speak through walls.

She climbed, carrying two folded truths: one naming the city’s deliberate sacrifices, the other naming her own.

chapters.name: The Testimony
chapters.content:
The courtroom had no windows.

Mara remembered that first, though the clerks insisted the chamber faced east and received morning light through a high band of salt glass. In her memory, the glass was black. The lamps beneath it burned without flame, and every face floated in a pale reflection above its body, as if the court had been assembled twice: once to judge her, and once to watch itself judging.

She remembered the smell of wet wool. Brass polish. The sour mineral stink of the flood still trapped in the walls.

She remembered not remembering.

“State your name.”

“Mara Venn.”

“Occupation.”

“Signal engineer.”

“Former signal engineer,” the prosecutor corrected. “Saboteur. Agitator. Leader of the Bellmaker cell.”

The words came in fragments, dislodged from different days. Sometimes the prosecutor was a woman with a silver tooth. Sometimes he was an old man whose voice clicked like a relay. Sometimes Halvek himself stood beneath the Council seal and read the charges in the patient tone he used for emergency announcements.

Mara Venn, architect of the Night of Bells.

Mara Venn, murderer of Kestrel.

Mara Venn, enemy of the city.

The casualty lists were stacked on a table beside the judges. They were bound in red cord, one volume for each district, though the numbers had been copied and recopied until the ink bled into the paper.

“Saint Orra: four hundred and twelve confirmed dead.”

“Eastern rail bridge: six hundred and eight.”

“Mercy Market: one hundred and ninety-three.”

“Lantern Ward: unverified losses estimated at—”

The prosecutor paused there. He looked toward the benches, where families sat with their hands folded over one another’s wrists.

“—one thousand, three hundred.”

A murmur moved through the chamber.

Mara stared at the lists. She knew some of the numbers were false. Not false in the simple way of invented things, but shaped. Inflated here, reduced there, made to carry the weight the Council required. The dead had become columns in a structure built to stand over her.

“Do you dispute the figures?” the prosecutor asked.

“No.”

The answer surprised the room.

“You accept responsibility for these deaths?”

“I accept that they happened.”

A laugh came from the gallery. It had no amusement in it.

The judges leaned toward one another. Mara saw their reflected faces above them, silent and weightless.

The prosecutor lifted a sheet. “On the night of the eighteenth, you and your accomplices gained access to four municipal warning towers. You altered the signal relays and introduced explosive charges into the maintenance locks.”

“Yes.”

“You synchronized the towers.”

“Yes.”

“You did so despite being warned that Saint Orra’s counterweight was unstable.”

Mara said nothing.

The courtroom sharpened around that silence.

A witness was called. He had been a maintenance worker at Saint Orra, or perhaps he had only worn the gray coat of one. His left cheek was wrapped in linen. He described the first bell. He described the tower shuddering. He described the canal wall opening as though a mouth had been cut into it.

“Did the accused give an order to proceed?” the prosecutor asked.

The worker looked at Mara.

“She said the city had waited long enough.”

“Did she know the mechanism was unsafe?”

“She knew there was a warning.”

“Did she stop?”

“No.”

In another fragment, the witness was a woman from Kestrel, her hair plastered to her face by floodwater. She held a child’s shoe in both hands. She said Mara had called the people toward Northern Avenue through the emergency speakers.

“She told us the route was open,” the woman said.

Mara remembered the speakers. She had patched the channel herself. She remembered saying, Go north. The avenue will clear. She had believed it. Or she had needed to believe it, because the alternative was that she had sent thousands toward a barricade she knew nothing about.

“Were the soldiers there?” Mara asked.

The prosecutor objected.

The judges allowed the question.

The woman’s mouth tightened. “Yes.”

“Did they open the avenue?”

“No.”

“Did they fire?”

The woman looked down at the shoe.

“Yes.”

The prosecutor rose. “The witness has established that the accused directed the crowd.”

“She has established that the Council barricaded the route,” Mara said.

“Your Honor—”

“She has established that armed men fired on people who followed my warning.”

The chief judge struck the desk with his mallet. The sound rang too cleanly. For an instant Mara was back beneath the eastern rail bridge, hearing the first tower answer from across the city.

One bell.

Then another.

Then the whole city opening its throat.

The Council did not produce the evacuation orders.

Mara asked for them on the second day of testimony. She asked where the northern trains had gone at nineteen-forty, three minutes before the first tower rang. She asked why the relief barges had been removed from Mercy Market and the old tram depot. She asked why Kestrel’s intakes had been classified nonessential six months before the flood.

The prosecutor called the questions inflammatory.

The judges called them irrelevant.

“No evidence has been submitted,” the chief judge said, “that any such orders existed.”

“They existed,” Mara said.

“You have seen them?”

“I helped uncover them.”

“Where are they?”

“Destroyed or sealed by the Council.”

“Then you ask this court to convict an absent authority on the basis of your word.”

“I ask you to look.”

“We are looking at you.”

That sentence survived in her better than any verdict.

The terrified witnesses were permitted to speak because their terror belonged to the prosecution. A father described finding his sons beneath a collapsed shelter gate. A woman from South Hook said the water rose while municipal pumps screamed in the wrong direction. An officer testified that the resistance had caused panic and made rescue impossible.

The officer did not mention that his unit had been ordered to hold Northern Avenue.

When Mara asked, he claimed not to remember.

When she asked who had issued the order, the judges removed the question from the record.

The record became a second courtroom, one Mara could not enter.

On the fourth day, Tomas Vale was called.

He wore a dark investigator’s coat, though he had not yet accepted his Council appointment. Or perhaps he had. Memory would not hold him still. In one version, he stood thinner than he had been, with a split lip and a bruise along his jaw.
