Mara stepped closer to the diagram. Water swirled around her boots, tugging toward the open Eastern channel. She traced the old line with one finger, then the newer one.

“The engine isn’t only a balance system,” she said. “It’s a selection system.”

Oris gave a breathless laugh. “We established that when it tried to kill us.”

“No. Look.”

She pointed to the pressure marks around the central wheel. Each channel had a graduated series of notches. The lowest was marked with a symbol for civilian districts. Above it were marks for storage, transit, and—higher still—something that had been scraped away.

Tomas leaned over the diagram. “What does that last symbol say?”

“Elevation,” Mara said. “Or refuge.”

The distinction had once mattered. In the old city plans, elevation meant high ground. Refuge meant people permitted to reach it.

She turned toward the northern channel. “The gates can reverse the distribution.”

Oris stared at her. Understanding moved across his face, followed by horror. “The North Basins are above the lower districts.”

“Not just above. They are connected to every protected reservoir in the upper city. Kestrel intakes. Lantern Ward hospitals. The Council’s emergency stores.”

“And if we close Lower and open North…” Tomas began.

“The surge climbs.” Mara looked at the dark mouth of the northern channel. “It would go where the Council designed the water not to go.”

Aven’s expression hardened. “Into the towers.”

“Into the towers,” Mara said.

For one suspended moment, the chamber seemed to breathe with her.

She imagined the upper city under warning bells. Glass walkways filling with brown water. The polished courts of North Basin reflecting the sky as they sank. Council houses with their sealed gardens, their private cisterns, their lamps burning behind high windows while the lower wards drowned. She imagined Ardin hearing the first impact from a room built above every remembered flood line.

The image did not frighten her.

That was what frightened her.

A pulse moved through the water. Somewhere beneath the platform, the unknown signal answered.

Three strikes.

A pause.

Three strikes.

The sound traveled through Mara’s bones like an invitation.

“Can you do it?” Aven asked.

Oris swallowed. “The original engine can. The new array has been welded into the distribution spine. If we break the lower lock and reset North, the pressure will choose the highest open route.”

“Can you do it?” Aven repeated.

“With time.”

The chamber shook. Dust sifted from the ceiling. In the west gallery, Juno fired twice into the dark. Someone cried out beyond the pillars.

“We have no time,” Tomas said.

Mara looked at the North wheel. Its spokes were thick enough to stand on, its iron teeth bright with recent oil. It was the largest of the three. Once opened, it would send the flood through the upper arteries of Veyr.

She could almost hear the city’s delight.

Not the people’s. The city’s—the old machinery of judgment, which required a culprit and a punishment and called the shape of suffering justice. She had believed for twelve years that Veyr secretly loved monsters because monsters made cruelty legible. A monster could be blamed. A monster could be displayed. The crowd could point and feel clean.

Now she saw the temptation from the other side.

Give them the flood.

Let the protected learn what protection cost.

Let the districts that had watched South Hook die stand in water up to their mouths. Let the Council’s ledgers become testimony written in ruined stone.

“Mara,” Tomas said.

She turned on him. “You know what this is.”

“I know what it looks like.”

“It looks like consequence.”

“It looks like another population being declared expendable.”

“By whom?” Her voice struck the chamber harder than the bells. “By the Council? They made the choice already. They made it every time they shortened the seawall. Every time they marked a ward sacrificial. Every time they sent relief north and called the dead unavoidable.”

“And you would make the same choice.”

“I would reverse theirs.”

“No.” Tomas stepped toward her, water breaking around his shins. “You would preserve the old shape and change the names.”

The words landed with an intimacy more painful than accusation. He had always known where to place them.

Mara saw him as he had been beneath the first warning tower, twelve years younger, sleeves rolled to his elbows, his hands black with cable grease. He had said, Wait. The maintenance lock is unstable. She had heard, You are afraid. She had heard, The Council wins if we hesitate.

The engine gave another shudder. From the northern bridge came the scrape of metal as one of Aven’s guides tried to fit a wrench to the wheel housing.

“Mara,” Ilya called, “the water is above the platform supports.”

“I know.”

“Then decide.”

She looked from Ilya to Oris, to the guides, to Juno in the west gallery. The people around her had surrendered blood, strength, and choice to reach this chamber. Their faces were not a crowd’s face. None of them wanted the same thing.

Aven wanted the lower enclaves alive.

Juno wanted her people out.

Oris wanted the engine stabilized, though he had not yet said what stabilization meant.

Ilya wanted no one treated as a number.

Tomas wanted—

“What do you want?” Mara asked him.

He flinched.

The chamber seemed to narrow around them, as if the stone itself had been waiting for the question.

“You want me to say it?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“I want this to mean something.”

“That is not an answer.”

“I want the records opened. I want Ardin tried. I want the names of the dead restored to the city that erased them.” His jaw tightened. “And I want you to believe that I did not spend twelve years inside the Council only to save myself.”

“You did save yourself.”

“Yes.”

The admission startled even the people who had not been listening.

Tomas looked down at the water. “I saved myself. I took the salary. I took the apartment. I signed the reports. I let them make you into the whole story because I thought I could preserve enough evidence to break the story later.”

“You thought history would forgive you.”

“I thought history might be useful.”

“You hid the warning.”

“I did.”

“You let me carry eight hundred dead people alone.”

His face broke then—not dramatically, not in a way that offered her the satisfaction of a wound. It simply lost its practiced structure.

“I know,” he said.

“You came to my cell with the Council’s sacrifice plans and still testified against me.”

“I testified to what you did.”

“You testified so they could call me the Bellmaker.”

“They already had the name.”

“You fed it.”

“Yes.”

The word hung between them.

Mara wanted him to defend himself. She wanted him to say he had been threatened, that his family had been held over him, that he had only chosen the least terrible path. Those things were true. They were also insufficient. She knew this because the truth had become intolerable when it carried only one blade.

“You want forgiveness,” she said.

Tomas shut his eyes briefly. “Yes.”

The water rose another inch.

Mara laughed once. It came out raw. “For what? For hiding the Council’s crimes? For letting me become their convenient monster? For using my name now to make your evidence admissible?”

“For all of it.”

“And you think the flood will cleanse you?”

“No.”

“Then why stop me?”

“Because my guilt does not give me the right to choose who dies.”

She stared at him.

“Neither does yours,” he said.

Behind him, Oris made a small sound. Ilya lowered him onto the edge of the platform and began wrapping a strip of cloth around his leg. The current tugged harder now, drawn toward the open Eastern Return. The old machinery was waking, and it would not care what moral language they used over its gears.

Mara moved to the central control.

There were three levers, each with a brass tag. EASTERN RETURN was down. NORTH BASINS stood upright but locked. LOWER CITY had been forced open by the Council’s new array.

If she opened North and closed Lower, the pressure would reverse. The first shock would travel through the elevated districts before the engine could balance itself. The Council’s own defenses would become channels of punishment.

It might save South Hook.

It might drown half the upper city.

It might do both.

She placed her hand on the North lever.

At once, the chamber filled with another sound: not the three-three signal, but a faint chorus of bells from far above. Warning towers answering one another across Veyr. The network was still connected. Somewhere, people were listening.

Mara imagined seizing it. She could tell them the truth, or enough of it. She could name the Council and let the upper districts feel the first wave of fear before the water arrived.

A clean story. A clean enemy.

Her fingers tightened around the lever.

“I can open it,” she said.

Tomas did not move. “I know.”

“Then people in the lower wards live.”

“Some.”

“More than if we leave it as it is.”

“Maybe.”

She turned toward him. “You object to the mathematics?”

“I object to pretending the mathematics absolves us.”

“People will die either way.”

“Yes.”

“And you have a better answer?”

“No.”

It should have enraged her. Instead, the absence of an answer steadied something inside her. The old Mara would have treated uncertainty as sabotage. She would have made a command out of it, forced the world into a shape that could be blamed on someone else.

Listen first. Then choose.

The principle did not make the choice clean. It only prevented her from calling cleanliness justice.

She released the North lever.

Tomas’s shoulders dropped, though he did not look relieved.

“We keep Lower open?” Aven asked.

“No,” Mara said. “Not yet.”

His eyes sharpened. “What are you doing?”

“Balancing all three channels.”

Oris lifted his head. “That is impossible in the reduced configuration.”

“Not impossible. Unstable.”

“It could shear the engine.”

“It could.”

“And the city?”

“Will take what the engine can give it.”

Tomas came nearer. “Mara.”

She faced him fully. “I am not choosing the upper city as punishment. I am not choosing the lower city because the Council chose it first. We open what can be opened, close what can be closed, and keep the pressure moving until the engine or the city tells us what remains.”

“That could save neither.”

“Yes.”

The word was quiet.

Juno shouted from the gallery. “They’re coming back!”

Gray figures appeared between the columns, their lamps shuttered, rifles raised. Juno fired and missed. Aven’s guides pulled Oris toward the North bridge.

Mara looked at Tomas. “Can you reach the signal cabinet?”

“I can.”

“Then connect every pressure line. No selective broadcast.”

His expression changed. “You’re certain?”

“No.” She turned toward the central wheel. “I am responsible for the choice. That is different.”

The three-three signal sounded again beneath them.

Three strikes.

A pause.

Three strikes.

This time, from somewhere in the eastern wall, another bell answered.

Mara seized the first wheel. Its iron rim was slick beneath her hands. The engine groaned, and the water surged to her knees.

“Eastern first,” Oris gasped.

“Already open.”

“North second.”

Mara looked across the flooded chamber at Tomas, at Ilya holding Oris upright, at Aven’s guides preparing to cross, at Juno firing one-handed into the approaching dark.

“North second,” she said.

Then she pulled.

chapters.name: The Broadcast
chapters.content:
The North wheel moved one inch and stopped.

Mara braced both feet against the grating. Water pressed around her knees, cold above and hot below where the engine’s buried heat rose through the chamber. The wheel’s spokes shuddered beneath her hands. Somewhere inside the wall, a tooth struck a tooth and refused to pass.

“Again,” Oris called.

His voice came thinly from the eastern platform. Aven and two Mercy Market guides had him between them, one arm over each shoulder. His face was gray from the chemical water, his pressure meter hanging uselessly against his chest. Ilya followed with her knife drawn, watching the gallery rather than the engineer.

Mara leaned into the wheel.

The ancient mechanism answered with a groan that seemed to come from under the city.

Above them, the warning bells began to ring.

Not the full peal. Three strikes. A pause. Three strikes.

The sound traveled through the chamber’s iron bones and entered Mara’s teeth. For twelve years she had heard that rhythm in dreams, in pipes, in the measured footsteps of guards outside her cell. Now an answering bell sounded from the eastern wall, deeper and farther away.

Three.

Pause.

Three.

The North wheel turned.

A burst of water tore through the lower sluice. The pressure struck Mara sideways. She caught the spoke and held on while the chamber blurred into spray and brass. On the far gallery, a gray-armored figure raised a hand cannon.

“Down!” Juno shouted.

Her pistol cracked from the west gallery. The agent spun backward, striking the rail. Juno’s wounded leg buckled, but she caught herself against the wall and fired again. Her second shot struck the gallery floor.

More gray figures entered behind the first.

“They’re through,” Tomas said.

He stood at the signal cabinet, one hand buried in its open housing. Wires trembled around his wrist. Blood from a cut at his temple ran down his cheek and disappeared into his collar.

“Can you hold the cabinet?” Mara called.

“For a little while.”

“Hold it.”

“That is not a measurement.”

“It is the only one we have.”

The North wheel turned another quarter span. A deep vibration passed through the chamber. On the indicator wall, three needles jerked upward: EASTERN RETURN, NORTH BASINS, LOWER CITY. None settled. All trembled in the red.

The engine was trying to choose.

Mara thought of South Hook shelter, eight hundred people packed behind gates built for four hundred and twelve. She remembered the noise they made against the doors. Not screaming, at first. They had struck in patterns, believing someone outside was listening.

Three strikes.

Pause.

Three strikes.

She had told herself the sound was accusation. She had made it proof of the Council’s cruelty. She had never asked whether it was also a plea.

A blue light flared above Tomas’s cabinet.

Every bell in the chamber stopped.

Then Mara heard her own voice.

“People of Veyr,” it said, carried through the old brass horns and the newer signal lines alike. “This is Mara Venn, the Bellmaker.”

The voice was perfect. Not merely her pitch, but the small rasp beneath it, the deliberate pauses, the breath she took before saying a difficult thing. Ardin had possessed twelve years of her speeches, trial records, prison interrogations. He had built a ghost from them.

“I have resumed my attack on the city. The Council offered me mercy, and I used its trust to enter the floodworks. I have opened the ancient engine. The southern districts will be sacrificed first. If the upper city does not submit to my demands, I will turn the water north.”

A crackle crossed the transmission. In the distance, beyond the chamber walls, bells began to ring in confusion.

“I did this before. I will do it again. The dead of South Hook were necessary. The weak are always the price of change.”

Mara’s fingers tightened on the North wheel.

The words were shaped like her old convictions. Their bones were hers. Their cruelty belonged to someone else.

“The Bellmaker has returned,” the false voice said. “Flee the lower city if you can. Those who remain have chosen their fate.”

The signal cut out.

For one breath there was only the engine.

Then a new voice entered the lines, frantic and distant. A woman shouting from an elevated district. Another voice ordering barricades closed. Somewhere, a bell rang without rhythm. Somewhere else, glass shattered.

Tomas pulled his hand from the cabinet.

“Ardin,” he said.

“No,” Mara replied. “Ardin is using the city.”

Aven appeared at the edge of the eastern platform, soaked to the waist. “The upper districts are closing their bridges. We can see smoke above Kestrel.”

“Smoke?”

“Riots, maybe. People are breaking into the storehouses.”

Tomas looked toward the signal cabinet. “The patrols will hear that broadcast as an order. They’ll abandon the lower wards.”

Mara saw it before he finished: armored boats turning away from flooded streets, rescue crews recalled to defend elevated gates, red lamps extinguished one by one. She saw the Council’s clean arithmetic continue beneath the lie. Bellmaker. Contamination. Necessary containment. Sacrificial occupancy.

The old story did not need to be true. It only needed to be familiar.

“Mara,” Ilya said, “can you take the network?”

Tomas looked at her. “We can seize the central signal, perhaps. But Ardin has the civic repeaters. If we cut him out, we may lose the lines entirely.”

“And if we don’t?”

“They keep hearing him.”

Mara turned from the wheel. The North mechanism groaned behind her, shivering under the rising pressure. The water had reached her thighs.

On the cabinet, a narrow glass panel showed the surviving channels. There were fewer than the original system had carried. Flooded towers. Broken relays. Dead districts. Still, dozens remained: upper markets, military frequencies, hospital bands, private signal houses, labor registries, the old warning towers.

Enough to make a weapon.

She could speak only to the upper city. She could give them the Council’s records, name the redirected seawalls, show them the words SACRIFICIAL and NONESSENTIAL OCCUPANCY. She could let the protected districts hear how their safety had been purchased.

She could say nothing about the unstable lock.

Nothing about the charge she had altered.

Nothing about the shelter gates.

The city would hate Ardin. It might even hate the Council. The dead would be counted under a different heading, and her name would remain clean enough to use.

Tomas was watching her.

He knew the shape of the silence she was considering.

“Do it,” he said.

Mara looked at him. “You want the records released.”

“I want the truth released.”

“Your truth.”

His mouth tightened. “No. Not if it excludes you.”

The gray agents emerged again on the north gallery. One carried a signal rifle. Another dragged a wounded Mercy guide by the collar. Juno fired from the west, forcing them behind a pillar.

“Hurry,” Ilya said.

Mara faced the cabinet.

“Tomas, open every surviving channel.”

He stared at her. “Every one?”

“Upper city, lower city, military, hospital, private. Warning towers. Any line with power.”

“That will make the signal unstable.”

“Yes.”

“It may carry no farther than this chamber.”

“Then we speak to this chamber.”

Aven’s expression hardened. “And if it carries everywhere?”

Mara put both hands on the cabinet’s copper frame. It hummed against her palms.

“Then everyone hears.”

Tomas did not move.

She understood why. He expected a demand, a command disguised as necessity. He expected her to appoint herself the only voice capable of saving Veyr.

“Listen first,” she said. “Then choose.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

He began pulling levers.

The network woke in fragments. Lamps flared across the cabinet: green, amber, red. Tomas patched a military line through the hospital band. He bridged the old warning towers to the civic repeaters. Wires spat blue sparks. The false voice returned in bursts, repeating the last sentence over and over.

Those who remain have chosen their fate.

Mara seized the speaking horn.

The first words nearly failed her. The horn magnified the chamber: water, gunfire, metal strain, her own breath.

“This is Mara Venn.”

Her voice went out.

The bells answered in scattered districts.

“I am speaking from beneath the flooded grain exchange. The broadcast claiming that I have resumed an attack is fabricated by Councilor Sere Ardin and the Civic Continuance office. The engine is open. The city is in danger. But I will not ask you to trust me because I say so.”

Tomas connected another line. A light burst white.

Mara continued.

“Twelve years ago, on the Night of Bells, I altered charges beneath the warning towers. I believed a simultaneous alarm would force the Council to reveal its evacuation plan. I believed fear could make power listen.”

The chamber seemed to contract around her.

“I was warned that the maintenance lock beneath Saint Orra was unstable. Tomas Vale warned me. I chose not to wait. I changed the design. When the towers rang, the lock failed. Saint Orra collapsed into the tide canal. The surge broke the chemical reservoirs. Power failed at South Hook shelter. The gates sealed.”

Her voice shook once. She let it.

“There were approximately eight hundred people inside. The shelter held four hundred and twelve. Many died because of the flood. Many died because the gates could not open. My actions helped make that failure possible. I did not order those deaths. I did not intend them. I caused devastation anyway.”

No one in the chamber moved.

Even the agents on the gallery had stopped firing.

Mara saw the shelter as it had been that night: hands against the gate, faces pale behind wired glass, a child lifted above the crowd so someone outside might see. She had searched for the control station while water climbed the walls. She had found the severed power lines. She had understood, too late, that the disaster was not merely something she had exposed.

It was something she had helped create.

“The Council also lied,” she said. “Before the Night of Bells, it shortened the South Hook seawall. It redirected Kestrel intakes and Lantern Ward relief. It protected the northern basins while marking southern neighborhoods SACRIFICIAL and NONESSENTIAL OCCUPANCY. It maintained evacuation ledgers for elevated residents and concealed them from everyone else.”

Tomas pushed a bundle of copied records into the cabinet’s document slot. The signal system accepted them with a grinding click.

“The records are now being transmitted. They include relocation orders, labor registration plans, Bell-Rat Clearance directives, redevelopment maps, and the current flood design. The Council has weighted the Lower City gate open and sealed the Eastern Return. It intends to direct this surge through South Hook, Lantern Ward, and Saint Orra’s lower districts, then clear the survivors into municipal labor camps.”

A sound rose somewhere beyond the chamber. Not a bell. Voices.

Mara imagined the broadcast moving through flooded tenements and guarded hospitals, through upper houses where people had gathered around private receivers to hear the monster confess. She imagined them searching the records, finding their own street names under red ink.

“I am not asking you to forgive me,” she said. “I am not asking you to call me a hero because the Council is criminal. The people who died because of my choices are still dead. The people the Council abandoned are still dead. One truth does not cancel the other.”

The engine gave a violent lurch.

The North wheel slipped beneath her hands.

“Hold it!” Oris shouted.

Mara caught the spoke. Water surged to her waist.

“The sequence is wrong,” Oris called. “Eastern first, North second, Lower last. We need the Lower gate moving before the pressure peaks.”

“Can you reset it?”

“Not from there!”

A gray agent stepped onto the north gallery and raised his rifle toward Tomas.

Mara released the horn and reached for the bell circuitry.

Three strikes sounded from the eastern wall.

Pause.

Three strikes.

The agent flinched. The ancient mechanism answered with a thunderous peal. The gallery lights burst. Darkness swallowed the north side, followed by a scream and the splash of someone falling.

“Mara!” Ilya shouted.

Mara seized the speaking horn again.

“To the guards in the lower districts: if you have orders to withdraw, understand what they mean. The Council is abandoning the people you were sworn to protect. You do not owe obedience to an order that names civilians expendable. To the people in the upper city: do not let them turn your fear against the flooded wards. Open your bridges. Open your stores. Listen to the records before you decide whom to hate.”

The signal crackled. Voices began to overlap: operators asking for confirmation, ward captains refusing withdrawal, a hospital administrator demanding to know whether the ledgers were genuine.

Then, clear through the interference, came a young man’s voice.

“My brother is in Lantern Ward,” he said. “Is this real?”

Mara closed her eyes.

“Yes,” she answered. “All of it is real.”

She opened them again and looked at Tomas.

“Transmit the names from South Hook.”

He nodded.

The first name entered the network. Then another. Tomas read from the list while Mara spoke each one into the horn. Eight hundred names where they had them. Names recovered from shelter rolls, workers’ tags, hospital ledgers, scraps found in the drowned streets. Some were incomplete. Some were marked unknown.

They did not make the dead less dead.

But they were no longer an empty number for the Council to spend, or a monument for Mara to hide behind.

Around the chamber, the bells continued to answer one another. Three strikes from the east. A reply from somewhere north. Then another from the dark below the engine platform.

The water rose.

Mara kept speaking.

She named the dead. She named the orders. She named herself.

chapters.name: Every Channel
chapters.content:
Water climbed over Mara’s waist.

The engine shuddered around her. Iron teeth struck iron somewhere beneath the platform, each impact traveling through the water and into her bones. The North wheel had moved a quarter span and stopped. Eastern Return burned green beneath a film of oil. Lower City trembled red.

“Lower,” Oris called from the eastern platform. His voice came thin through the chamber. “Mara, you have to start Lower now.”

“I know.”

“You have less than a minute.”

“I know.”

She held the transmission lever with one hand and the North wheel with the other. The wheel was warm despite the water. A current dragged at her legs, pulling toward the lower gate. Around her, the engine’s ancient channels opened and closed by fractions, undecided. The mechanism had been built to distribute pressure according to a hierarchy of districts. It knew how to choose who would be flooded.

It did not know what to do with refusal.

Mara leaned toward the speaking horn.

“South Hook shelter,” she said. “Capacity four hundred and twelve. Occupied approximately eight hundred on the night of the bells. The eastern gate failed after the Saint Orra lock collapsed. The gate failure was not only the Council’s work. My charges cut power to the control banks. I knew the lock was unstable. Tomas warned me. I proceeded.”

The words went out through every surviving channel.

In the upper city, they entered apartments where families had crowded around civic receivers, expecting another threat. In the lower wards, they crackled from hospital horns and warehouse speakers, through the signal houses that had not yet been seized. They reached patrol boats, guard stations, labor registries, and the old warning towers.

They reached Mercy Market by way of a wire strung between two chimney stacks.

They reached the soldiers in the west gallery.

They reached Councilor Sere Ardin.

Mara could not hear all those places, but the network gave back fragments. A woman in Lantern Ward shouting that the records were forged. A hospital operator demanding the names of the children on the rolls. A guard captain ordering his men to hold position. Someone laughing, high and frightened, saying the Bellmaker had learned to perform remorse.

Then a child’s voice came through the return line.

“Is this real?”

The voice belonged to a relay operator, perhaps, or to someone who had taken the instrument from one. It shook with the effort of being brave.

Mara looked at the water. It had reached the lower edge of the brass panel.

“All of it is real,” she said. “The Council’s ledgers. The shortened seawall. The orders marked SACRIFICIAL and NONESSENTIAL OCCUPANCY. My sabotage. The shelter rolls. The dead.”

Tomas’s voice entered from the signal cabinet, roughened by blood and static. “South Hook names are transmitting now.”

The first names followed.

Not a list, exactly. A stream of lives.

Pella An, dock clerk. Oren Vale, nine years old. Iseth and Marn Dorr, sisters. Unknown woman, blue coat, found beside the west gate. Three unnamed infants. A man carrying a red tin box. Hessa—

The line broke into a burst of white noise.

Mara’s grip tightened.

“Hessa?” she said.

“Partial record,” Tomas answered. “I’m restoring it.”

A bell struck in the eastern wall.

Three notes. A pause. Three notes.

The sound was so deep the water jumped.

Then, from far above, another bell answered.

The upper city’s alarm towers had not been connected to the old system in decades. The Council had disconnected them after the Night of Bells, declaring the antiquated network compromised. Yet the answer rolled down through the shaft, through stone and flooded masonry, until the chamber itself seemed to listen.

Across the city, other bells began to reply.

Mara imagined people stopping in the streets. Looking up. Waiting to be told what the sound meant.

For twelve years, Veyr had been given monsters because monsters were simpler than choices.

“Listen first,” she whispered.

“What?” Oris called.

“Nothing.”

A red lamp flared over the Lower City channel.

The engine had begun to take pressure.

Water struck Mara’s ribs. The North wheel wrenched beneath her palm. She let it slip rather than lose her fingers, then caught the spoke again.

“Lower gate,” Oris said. “It’s binding.”

“Can you reach the reset?”

“Not from here.”

“Ilya?”

“I’m coming.”

Her answer came from below the eastern platform. A moment later, Ilya appeared waist-deep in the water, dragging a cable behind her. Two Mercy Market guides followed, each carrying a red lamp wrapped in oilskin. Aven, the eldest of them, had a blood-dark bandage around his head.

“Your people stay out of the chamber,” Mara said.

Aven looked at the flooding floor, then at the gate controls. “They are our people too.”

“Then get them to the diversion array.”

“The array is sealed.”

“Not for long.”

Ilya seized the cable from her. “The lower controls are beyond that grate.”

“That passage is unstable.”

“You just said not for long.”

Mara started to answer, but Ilya had already turned away. She and the guides pushed through the water toward the eastern trench.

Juno’s pistol cracked from the west gallery.

The sound ricocheted across the chamber. A gray-armored figure fell from the catwalk and disappeared without a splash.

“More coming!” Juno shouted. “And my ammunition is becoming theoretical!”

Mara looked toward the gallery. Juno knelt behind a corroded housing, one leg twisted under her, firing one-handed. Two of her remaining guards held the barricade. Beyond them, gray helmets moved through the steam.

A second voice cut over the military channel.

“By order of Civic Continuance, all lower-city personnel withdraw to the north bridges. Repeat, withdraw. Flood containment is no longer viable. Leave the undercity. Repeat, abandon the lower wards.”

The voice was calm. It belonged to an official who had practiced sounding merciful.

Juno heard it through her receiver. For one second, she went still.

Then she pressed the transmitter.

“Identify the order.”

Static answered.

“Identify the authority,” she said.

A different guard came onto the line. “Captain, the relay says Council seal.”

“Not a name.”

“Council seal is sufficient.”

“Not anymore.”

One of the guards behind her lowered his rifle.

Juno looked at him. “You have a problem?”

“My sister is in Lantern Ward.”

“Then you know where the orders lead.”

The guard turned his rifle toward the north gallery.

Another guard followed.

A third said, “My mother’s at the Kestrel intake.”

The barricade shifted. Not backward. Outward.

Juno raised her voice over the channel. “Any unit receiving this order: if you abandon civilians, you are not containing a flood. You are enforcing a clearance. Choose whether you will carry that choice home.”

For a heartbeat, no one answered.

Then a signal house in the upper city broke in.

“This is Relay Seven,” a woman said. “We are receiving evacuation ledgers. They’re authentic. We have the Council’s archive stamp.”

Another voice followed, male and breathless. “Bridge patrol at Morningspan refusing withdrawal. We have opened the east barricade.”

“Hospital Three has patients from South Hook,” said a third. “We knew some of these names.”

A fourth voice spat, “This is Bellmaker theater. She’s confessing because she wants control of the gates.”

Mara closed her eyes.

There it was. The old argument, clean and useful. If she spoke, she manipulated. If she stayed silent, she plotted. A monster did not need to be believed. It needed only to remain available.

She opened her eyes and spoke into the horn.

“If you think this is manipulation, record everything anyway. Compare the ledgers. Test the measurements. Do not trust me because I confess. Do not trust the Council because I accuse it. Listen first. Then choose.”

The chamber lights flickered.

In the signal station above, Tomas stood before the main cabinet with one hand pressed to his temple. The old civic relay had been forced open, its copper guts spilling across the floor. Behind him, the flood stairs were filling with gray water.

Ardin’s face appeared in the central mirror, pale and magnified by the relay lens.

“You have made a spectacle of her,” Ardin said.

Tomas wiped blood from his eye. “You made her a spectacle twelve years ago.”

“I gave Veyr a name for the dead.”

“You gave Veyr someone to blame.”

“Because she was responsible.”

“She was responsible for part of it.”

“Part is enough when the dead are counted.”

“Then count your part.”

Ardin’s expression barely altered. That was his gift: the ability to receive horror as an administrative inconvenience.

“You think disclosure will save you?” he asked. “The upper districts are rioting. Food stores are being opened by force. Guards are refusing lawful orders. You have not exposed a conspiracy. You have dissolved the city.”

“The city was already dissolved. You only kept the pieces in separate rooms.”

“You are assisting a terrorist.”

Tomas glanced toward the open channel. “She is naming what she did.”

“She is using the flood to launder her guilt.”

“No,” Tomas said. “That was your method.”

Ardin’s voice sharpened. “You signed the report.”

“Yes.”

“You accepted exemption for your family.”

“Yes.”

“You remained in Council service.”

“Yes.”

The admissions traveled through the live channel. Mara heard them in the engine chamber, stripped of argument.

Tomas leaned closer to the mirror.

“I did those things. I told myself I was preserving evidence. Sometimes I was. Sometimes I was afraid. Sometimes I wanted the comfort of being useful to the people who had already decided what I was worth. Put that in the record too.”

Ardin reached for something beyond the frame.

The signal cabinet gave a hard metallic click.

Tomas looked down. “What did you do?”

“Nothing that will matter.”

Every civic repeater in Veyr went silent.

For one terrible instant, there was only the engine, the water, and the distant bells.

Then the old network opened.

Mara’s voice returned from beneath the city, doubled and distorted.

“South Hook shelter…”

The names resumed from where they had broken.

Hessa—

The line dissolved again, but another operator caught it.

“Hessa Venn,” a woman said. “Shelter intake, row fourteen. Age forty-three. Occupation—school cook.”

Mara’s breath stopped.

The name was not hers. Hessa had been the one who taught her to read tide tables, the one who called every reckless plan a child’s tantrum and every apology too late. Mara had searched for her after the flood until the tunnels filled with bodies and lamp oil.

“Hessa Venn,” Tomas repeated, softer.

The name went through the city.

Something inside Mara tried to turn it into a symbol. Proof of the Council’s cruelty. Proof of the cost of resistance. Proof that she had been abandoned before she had abandoned anyone.

She refused.

“Hessa Venn,” Mara said into the horn. “Dead at South Hook. I did not kill her with my hands. My choices helped make the conditions in which she died. That distinction matters for the record. It does not return her.”

The Lower indicator shook violently.

“Mara!” Oris shouted. “Now!”

She released the North wheel.

It spun back half a turn.

Mara plunged both hands into the water and found the Lower gate’s emergency lever by touch. It was locked beneath a collar of rust. She braced one foot against the housing and pulled.

Nothing.

Again.

The metal groaned.

From the eastern trench came a flare of red light. Ilya and Aven had reached the diversion controls. The guides crowded behind them, hauling at the sealed grate. Beyond it, the newly installed array pulsed with the Council’s blue-white lamps.

“Open it!” Mara yelled.

“We’re trying!”

“Not trying. Choose.”

Aven looked back at her through the steam. “You think words make people move?”

“No. People do.”

He nodded once and turned to the grate.

On the military channel, Juno’s voice came through, strained but steady. “North gallery secured. Two patrols have joined us. Gray agents retreating toward the signal stairs.”

Tomas answered from above. “They are not retreating. Ardin is routing them to the cabinet.”

“Then hold them.”

“I will.”

A gunshot cracked over his transmission.

The mirror feed vanished.

“Tomas?” Mara called.

Only static.

The Lower lever shifted a finger’s width.

The engine answered with a roar.

Water surged through the chamber, throwing Mara against the housing. The flood rose to her chest. Somewhere below, a lock opened with a sound like a mountain splitting.

The Lower indicator moved from red toward amber.

Not safe. Not balanced. Moving.

Ilya’s crew tore the grate free. One of the guides screamed as the current caught him, but Aven seized his coat and hauled him back. They reached the diversion controls together.

“Which gate?” Ilya shouted.

Mara looked at the three trembling lamps.

“Eastern Return first,” she said. “Keep it open. North second. Lower last. Do not close a gate because it protects someone. Close it only if opening it destroys everyone.”

The words felt too small for the mechanism, too human for the pressure gathering beyond the walls.

Aven placed both hands on the Eastern wheel.

“What if we cannot hold all three?”

“Then tell the truth about which one fails.”

“Your truth?”

“No,” Mara said. “Everyone’s.”

Across Veyr, the bells continued answering one another.

From the upper city came a burst of voices: guards reporting opened bridges, civilians breaking storehouse seals, hospital workers refusing relocation orders. Beneath them, lower districts sent back their own sounds—pipe taps, shouted names, boat horns, the pounding of people refusing to disappear quietly.

Ardin’s voice returned on one remaining channel, no longer composed.

“Shut the lower line,” he ordered. “Mara, shut it now. You can still preserve the northern basins.”

Mara saw the old map in her mind. North protected. Lower sacrificed. A clean decision made by someone far from the water.

She tightened her hands on the lever.

“No.”

“You will kill thousands.”

“I may.”

“Then you are exactly what I said.”

Mara looked at the black water rushing through the open channels.

“No,” she said. “The difference is that I will not call the killing necessary before I have tried to prevent it.”

She pulled the lever another inch.

The engine screamed.

The next bell struck from beneath the platform.

Three notes. A pause. Three notes.

Every surviving channel carried the sound.

chapters.name: The Reduced Configuration
chapters.content:
The engine did not fail all at once.

A tooth sheared beneath the platform. A valve screamed and held. The eastern channel flashed white, then darkened to old blood. The mechanism strained against itself, pressure rising in one throat while another emptied.

Mara held the Lower emergency lever with both hands.

Water had reached her ribs. It shoved against her from the open gate, carrying splinters, insulation, and a dead lamp that struck her hip. Above the roar, the bells continued their pattern.

Three strikes.

Pause.

Three strikes.

The eastern bell had answered first. Then one in the upper city, though that tower had been disconnected for generations. More bells joined from beneath the platform and beyond the drowned districts. Not an alarm now. A question repeated until Veyr had no choice but to hear it.

“What’s the reading?” Mara shouted.

Oris knelt at the instrument housing, dragging a grease pencil through streaming numbers. “Eastern holding at forty-two. North rising too fast. Lower is binding.”

“Binding how?”

“The gate’s taking pressure from both sides.”

“Then it’s balanced.”

“It’s tearing.”

A crack traveled through the chamber. The floor lurched. A section of outer gallery dropped into the tidal cavern, taking three gray agents and one survivor with it. Their shouts vanished in the dark.

Ilya appeared through the spray, dragging a boy by the collar. Aven and six Mercy Market guides followed, carrying tools, rope, and wounded people.

“Eastern grate is open,” Ilya said. “We have two hands on North, but the wheel is slipping.”

“Three hands,” Aven said. “One is broken.”

“Can you move it?”

“We can move it. We can’t hold it.”

Mara looked at the indicators.

NORTH BASINS: amber, flickering toward red.

EASTERN RETURN: green, wavering.

LOWER CITY: red, edging toward amber.

She had moved North a quarter span before releasing it when Lower began to bind. She had broken the Lower emergency lever loose and shifted it another inch. The engine had answered by trying to tear itself apart.

A total opening might divide the pressure and save every district.

It might also send the force into the central throat. The cavern would rise through the foundations, splitting the engine and everyone near it.

“How long?” Mara asked.

Oris knew what she meant. “Until it shears? Minutes. Maybe less.”

“And if we keep shifting the gates?”

“We might get a stable sequence.”

“Might.”

“If North holds.”

“If it doesn’t?”

“The upper basins flood before the lower ones drain.”

Juno’s voice came through the speaking tube from the west gallery. “Mara.”

The sound was rough with static. Mara pictured her there: one hand on her pistol, the other pressed to the hole through her thigh, guards crouched behind overturned conduit while gray agents tried to cross.

“Report.”

“We’re losing the west brace. Official order says all personnel are to withdraw from the lower wards.”

“Who issued it?”

“Seal of Civic Continuance.”

“That isn’t an authority.”

“I know.” Gunfire thundered through the tube, followed by a cheer and a cry. “Two patrols have joined us. They have families in Lantern Ward. They’re asking whether we’re holding for the upper city or the lower.”

Mara shut her eyes.

The question wanted an answer shaped like a district.

“Tell them we’re holding for whoever can still be reached.”

“That sounds like something you’d say before making the choice yourself.”

“I am making it.”

“Then say it clearly.”

Mara opened her eyes. She could close Eastern and protect the northern basins. The upper city had elevation, walls, hospitals, and food stores. More people lived there.

That was the arithmetic the Council had used.

She could open North fully and send the surge toward the high districts. That would be vengeance dressed in numbers.

Or she could force all three channels open and let the machinery decide, calling the wreckage fate.

“Listen first,” she said into the broadcast line.

The bells fell silent.

For one breath, the city waited.

“The engine cannot save every structure,” Mara said. “Pressure has exceeded the original design. If we open every channel, the chamber will rupture and take the lower and upper basins together. If we close Eastern, the lower districts will be abandoned. If we open North beyond the safe span, the water will be directed into the elevated wards.”

Oris stared at her. “Mara—”

She raised a hand.

“The surviving controls can be set to a reduced configuration. Eastern Return stays open. North takes only what the structure can hold. Lower opens last, as far as the braces allow.”

Aven shouted from the grate, “What does that save?”

Mara read the trembling gauges. “Not all of Veyr.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” she said. “It is the truth.”

Voices crowded the line: operators, survivors, guards, people calling from streets that no longer had streets. Someone cursed her name.

Juno cut through them.

“You heard her. Move North to the marked notch. Not farther. If the notch breaks, stop pretending your arms can replace a wall.”

A guard answered, “We can’t hold it and get the families through.”

“Get the families through first.”

Mara turned to Oris. “Can you restart the sequence?”

“Restart is not the word.”

“Can you make it continue?”

“It has never obeyed anyone.”

“Then make it continue.”

He looked at the instruments. “We need the manual gate held at the west throat while Eastern catches.”

“Who holds it?”

Juno emerged from the west passage supported by two guards.

Her face was white. Blood diluted around her injured leg. In one hand she carried a short iron bar.

“No,” Mara said.

Juno ignored her. “Where?”

Oris pointed to the crooked gate. “The brace is failing. Someone must keep it from kicking closed until Eastern stabilizes.”

“How long?”

“Long enough.”

“That means nothing.”

“It means we don’t know.”

Juno handed the bar to a guard. “You know what I like about engineers? They make death sound like a measurement.”

Ilya reached for her. “Your leg—”

“My leg is already having a poor day.”

“You’ll bleed out.”

“Then work faster.”

Mara caught Juno’s arm. Beneath the soaked sleeve, the muscles were rigid with pain.

“You don’t get to decide your life is the acceptable loss.”

Juno’s eyes hardened. “Neither do you.”

The words struck through the noise.

“You want control?” Juno said. “Here is the part no one puts on a map. You cannot keep everyone alive. You can only refuse to lie about who you leave behind.”

Mara released her.

Juno crossed to the west throat. Guards fastened a rope around her waist and anchored it to a column. She wedged the iron bar into the gate’s lower teeth, then braced her shoulder against the handle.

“Now,” she called.

Oris pulled the starter chain.

Nothing happened.

He pulled again. The chain came free in his hand. The boy with the cable spool crawled beneath the housing and began reconnecting the severed line. Ilya shoved two survivors into position beside him, shouting instructions over the water. A woman with blood down her face climbed the North wheel and wrapped both arms around it.

The engine shook.

At the west throat, Juno screamed as the gate struck the bar. The rope snapped tight. One guard was thrown into the current. Juno’s wounded leg folded, but she drove herself upright.

“Eastern!” Oris shouted.

The lamp flared white.

Aven and the Mercy Market crews pulled the return valve together. It resisted, then released with a sound like a mountain cracking. Water spun backward through the eastern channel. The chamber pressure dropped by a fraction.

“North!”

The woman twisted the wheel to the marked notch. It slammed against its stop. Her shoulder popped, but she held on until three others replaced her.

“Lower!”

Mara pulled.

The lever moved another inch.

The engine roared. Water rose, fell, and surged again. Green light flashed through the cavern as the old channels woke.

The Lower gate opened.

The current tore through the chamber and carried two bodies into the dark. Mara felt the lever wrench beneath her hands. She held it until the metal cut her palms, then allowed it to move only as far as the amber mark.

“Enough!” Oris yelled. “Hold there!”

She held.

The instrument map redrew itself in trembling lines. Eastern stabilized. North carried pressure away from the central throat without taking it all. Lower opened toward Lantern Ward, South Hook, and Saint Orra’s drains.

Not safe.

Not fair.

Possible.

Through a ruptured viewing arch, Mara saw South Hook tilt into the flood. The shelter tower remained for one breath, its upper windows bright with movement. Then it folded inward. Water swallowed the market district and climbed through the lower streets.

Aven made a sound beside her.

“Keep the gate,” Mara said.

“That was my home.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

“No,” Mara said. “I don’t.”

The flood continued through the condemned districts. Lantern Ward lost its western bridge. Saint Orra’s lower terraces vanished beneath a boiling sheet of water. The engine divided the pressure, but division was not rescue. It was only a way to make survival possible for some.

Juno’s voice came through the static.

“Gate’s slipping!”

Mara turned.

The west brace had split. Juno hung against the manual handle, the rope cutting into her waist. Water struck her from behind. The iron bar had bent into a crescent.

“Pull her out!” Mara ordered.

Two guards ran toward the throat.

Juno saw them and shook her head. “No!”

“They can take the lever!”

“They can’t hold it.”

“I’m not leaving you.”

“You are if you want the configuration to hold.”

The guard nearest her reached for the rope. Juno kicked him back with her good leg.

“Get the survivors through,” she said. “That’s the order.”

“It isn’t an order,” Mara said.

Juno looked across the flooded platform. For the first time since leaving the Bastion, she smiled.

“Then call it a choice.”

The west gate buckled.

Juno drove the bar deeper into the teeth and locked both arms around it. The rope tore free. The guards stumbled backward as the current took her weight.

Mara moved toward her.

Ilya seized Mara’s coat. “If you leave the lever—”

“I know.”

Juno’s face vanished behind spray. Her voice came once more through the tube, broken but clear.

“Listen first.”

Then the gate slammed open.

The pressure changed. Eastern surged. North steadied. Lower remained amber, held just below the point where the engine would rip itself apart.

Juno vanished into the west throat.

For a while, no one spoke.

The engine continued to turn.

Mara kept her hands on the lever and watched the indicators settle into their reduced configuration: three uneven lights, none green, none red. Behind the chamber walls, Veyr broke along old boundaries and survived along others. Boats moved through streets. Shelter doors opened. Bells marked routes instead of deaths.

On the broadcast line, voices began naming the districts that had gone under.

Mara did not interrupt them.

She did not add Juno’s name to the list. Not yet. Water was not always proof. The chamber held many places to hide a body, and Mara had spent twelve years turning uncertainty into verdicts.

“Keep recording,” she said.

Oris looked at her. “The engine is holding.”

“For now.”

“For now is what we have.”

Mara faced the speaking tube.

“To every crew,” she said, “the reduced configuration is active. It will not save every district. Do not call the losses clean. Do not call them deserved. Mark every failed gate, every closed shelter, every name you can recover. If a route opens, tell people where it leads. If it closes, tell them why.”

The bells answered from the dark.

Three strikes.

Pause.

Three strikes.

Mara listened as the surviving channels carried the sound into the drowned city. Then she looked down at her bleeding hands and held the lever steady while people escaped through the spaces the engine had left them.

chapters.name: No Forgiveness Yet
chapters.content:
By dawn, the engine no longer sounded like an animal tearing through the earth.

It turned with a slower, uneven labor. Eastern Return groaned beneath the platform. North held at its marked notch. Lower remained amber, drawing pressure through districts the Council had left to drown.

Mara kept both hands on the lever until Oris said, for the third time, “You can let go.”

“I know.”

“You’re bleeding on the brass.”

“I know that too.”

Ilya cut Mara’s palms free with a narrow knife and wrapped them in boiled cloth. “I’m doing this carefully,” she said, before Mara could object.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want you to die before the tribunal decides what to do with you.”

The lower gallery had become a place of lists. Every wall held chalk marks: failed gates, opened shelters, blocked routes, recovered names, names spoken by strangers, names no body had confirmed. Ilya made the crews record the living as well as the dead. Mara ordered the times beside every entry.

No one called the result a victory.

Above them, Veyr listened in the wrong kind of quiet. Not peace. Expectation.

Ardin had been arrested in the Hall of Measures. The guards who found him still wore gray, though they had removed the Council seals from their collars. He had protested on procedural grounds.

“What procedure?” Aven had asked the messenger.

“He said the city was not permitted to arrest its own continuity.”

Someone had laughed. Someone else had begun to cry.

Mara asked whether Tomas Vale was alive.

“Alive,” the boy said. “Shot in the shoulder, maybe. He walked out with his evidence case.”

That was all the certainty the city possessed.

For three days, survivors came from the remaining dry districts and the flooded ones. They arrived by boat, along roofs joined with planks, through reopened bridge arches. They brought blankets, bread, rumors, accusations, and the names of people who had not appeared.

Some came to see Mara.

A woman from Lantern Ward held a child against her hip and shouted, “You knew what the bells could do.”

“Yes.”

The woman flinched. “You knew.”

“I knew Tomas had warned me about the Saint Orra lock.”

“You did this.”

“Yes.”

The child began to whimper. The woman turned away.

A dockworker called Mara a butcher. An old priest asked whether she had repented. A girl with a split lip asked whether the bells had hurt when they rang.

Mara answered when she could. When she could not, she said so.

The people disliked that almost as much as they had disliked her silence.

On the fourth day, a provisional tribunal assembled in the upper hall of the old Customs Exchange. The lower floors had flooded, and the surviving room smelled of damp wool, lamp oil, and mold. No Council banners hung behind the judges. Blank canvas had replaced them.

The blankness was meant to signify a new authority.

Mara saw only an unclaimed surface.

Tomas sat beneath the windows. His left arm was strapped to his chest, and a strip of white cloth crossed his shoulder. Two clerks sat beside him with crates of records. He had brought the Council into the room in paper form.

Ardin stood behind a barred partition. Without his gray coat and seal, he seemed less like a man than the habit of one: straight-backed, bloodless, offended by consequence.

“Bellmaker,” he said as Mara entered.

The word moved through the hall like a thrown stone.

She sat at the witness table. Judge Pellin, a former harbor magistrate, asked whether she understood the proceedings.

“No.”

A murmur rose.

“You understand that this tribunal will determine responsibility for the flood, the Council’s emergency actions, and the deaths resulting from both?”

“I understand the words. I don’t know what authority means now.”

“That is why we are here.”

“No,” Mara said. “You are here because people need to hear who will decide.”

Pellin frowned. “And who should decide?”

“Everyone who was denied a choice.”

The hearing lasted until dark.

Tomas gave evidence first. He described the evacuation scheme, the shortened seawalls, the protected northern basins, and the classification of southern districts as sacrificial occupancy. He identified signatures and routing numbers. He explained how the Council had used the latest flood to establish relocation camps and municipal labor assignments.

Then he described himself.

“I altered maintenance records after the Night of Bells,” he said. “I concealed my warning about the Saint Orra lock. I accepted a Council appointment and protection for my family. I signed reports that allowed the public account to become simpler than the truth.”

A survivor shouted, “You let her take it!”

Tomas did not turn. “Yes.”

“You testified against her!”

“Yes.”

“You knew she hadn’t caused every death.”

“Yes.”

Ardin leaned toward the bars. “This is theater. A disgraced investigator laundering his cowardice through confession.”

Tomas looked at him. “You taught us that guilt was most useful when assigned to someone who could not return it.”

The guards struck the bars with their rifles.

“Enough,” Pellin said.

But no one believed enough existed anymore.

When the tribunal called Mara, she remained seated.

“I will speak,” she said, “but not as your witness.”

“You are not in a position to dictate terms.”

“Then record that I refused to be arranged.”

Pellin glanced at the gallery, then nodded to the clerk. “Proceed.”

Mara described the resistance’s original plan: seize the warning towers, broadcast the hidden evacuation orders, and force the Council to open routes. She described the first failure, the public outrage that had not moved power, and the anger that convinced her fear could make the city listen.

Then she described the charges.

“I knew Saint Orra’s lock was unstable. Tomas warned me. I chose to modify the charges so the towers would ring together. I believed spectacle would force the truth into every household. I believed fear could make power listen.”

A woman near the rear began to sob.

“The towers collapsed,” Mara continued. “The canal ruptured. Chemicals entered the flood. Power failed. Gates sealed. The surge reached South Hook. Eight hundred people were sheltering in a place built for four hundred and twelve. Hessa Venn was in intake row fourteen. She was forty-three. She had been my teacher.”

Her voice tightened. She waited, then went on.

“The Council created the conditions for abandonment. I created the event they used to complete it. These are not competing truths. They are both true.”

The gallery broke open.

“Hang her!”

“Use her! She knows the system!”

“Lock her back in the Bastion!”

“Let South Hook decide!”

“Let everyone decide!”

Mara listened. The city did not secretly want a monster. It wanted a shape for its grief. Sometimes that shape was her. Sometimes it was Ardin. Sometimes it was the blank canvas behind the judges.

When the hall quieted, Pellin read the tribunal’s proposal.

“Recognizing the extraordinary public necessity, the provisional authority offers Mara Venn immediate freedom from confinement, immunity from prosecution for acts connected to reconstruction of the warning network, and appointment as chief technical adviser to the civic restoration commission. Her testimony against the Council will be entered as full cooperation. In exchange, she will rebuild the warning system and submit to public review of all future directives.”

The old language had changed its coat. That was all.

“And if I refuse?” Mara asked.

“You remain subject to prosecution for mass manslaughter, sabotage, and unlawful destruction.”

“Will the Council officials receive similar immunity?”

“No.”

“Will Tomas?”

Pellin paused. “His case is separate.”

“Then this is not an offer. It is a bargain made with the dead absent from the room.”

“The city needs the warning system rebuilt,” Pellin said. “It needs people who know how.”

“Yes.”

“It needs you.”

Mara looked at the blank canvas. “The city needed me to make a choice before. I made one. People died. I will not turn necessity into a warrant.”

“You prefer imprisonment to service?”

“I prefer a process that does not make my usefulness erase my responsibility.”

In the gallery, Aven stood. Her face was gray with exhaustion. Her home was among the districts lost.

“If she refuses,” Aven said, “who repairs the bells?”

Mara looked at her.

“Someone else.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is the beginning of one. Open everything—the schematics, the failures, the decisions, the names. No sealed technical archives. No emergency authority without witnesses from the districts affected.”

“You are making demands of a tribunal offering you your life,” Pellin said.

“My life is not yours to offer.”

Silence settled over the hall.

Outside, a bell sounded once. Another answered across the river. A third rang from somewhere beneath the city.

Pellin dismissed the hearing until morning. Guards led Mara through a side passage, but no one locked her in a cell. They did not know whether she was prisoner, witness, engineer, or accused. Their uncertainty followed her like another escort.

At the Exchange doors, Ilya caught up.

“You refused freedom,” she said.

“I refused immunity.”

“You could still be executed.”

“Yes.”

“Does that feel like responsibility?”

“No. It feels like an outcome I cannot command.”

“And if they imprison you?”

“Then I will learn the shape of that.”

“And if they ask you to repair the bells?”

“I will repair them if the work can be watched, questioned, and interrupted.”

“That sounds like a yes.”

“It is not forgiveness.”

“I didn’t ask for forgiveness.”

“No,” Mara said. “You asked whether I thought death was responsibility.”

Ilya looked toward the river, where boats moved among the drowned roofs.

“Do you?”

Mara listened to the bells answering one another through Veyr. Some marked open shelters. Some marked missing people. Some carried the old three-strike rhythm from the dark network beneath the streets.

“No,” she said. “Death is only final.”

Behind them, the tribunal doors opened. A clerk emerged carrying the first ledger of names.

Mara stepped aside to let him pass.

She did not touch the book. She did not claim a place beside it. She watched as the clerk carried the dead into the hearing chamber, where the city would argue over what to do with her and call the argument justice.

Then Mara turned toward the engine stairs.

At the bottom, the lamps were still burning. Crews recorded pressure, closures, routes, and failures. No one waited for her to tell them what the truth meant.

She went down among them, carrying her unpardoned hands.

chapters.name: The Open Gate
chapters.content:
The first thing Mara repaired was not the bell.

It was the gate beneath it.

The iron hatch had warped under pressure, its hinges pulled half out of the wall. Someone had painted an arrow beside it, pointing down toward the engine stairs. Beneath the arrow, one hand had written CLOSED. Another had crossed the word out.

Mara rested her bandaged fingers against the stone.

“Leave it,” said the guard behind her.

“It opens inward,” she said. “When the pressure rises, anyone on the other side will be crushed against it.”

“I was told you were here to inspect the warning towers.”

“I am inspecting the gate.”

The guard wore no Council insignia. A strip of blue cloth marked him as provisional tribunal security, tied over a sleeve that still showed the pale outline of a removed seal. He held his rifle low, but not carelessly.

“Who gave you authority to alter doors?”

“Who gave you authority to prevent it?”

His jaw tightened. Mara knew that expression. She had once made a profession of finding the hesitation beneath it, then filling the hesitation with her own command.

“Write it down,” she said. “Gate opens inward. Hinge must be cut before the next pressure test. If you refuse, record that refusal beside the time.”

He took a slate from his belt. “Time?”

“Sixteen forty-three.”

“Name?”

“Mara Venn.”

He wrote it. Not Bellmaker. Not terrorist. The name gave her no protection, but neither did the titles.

Around them, crews moved along the engine stairs with ropes, lamps, and pressure gauges. Water struck the stone below. Every few minutes the eastern bell answered from above: three strikes, a pause, three strikes.

The sound passed through Mara’s ribs.

Aven crouched at the next landing, securing a cable around a cracked support. Ilya sat on an overturned crate, changing the dressing on Mara’s hands without asking.

“You’re bleeding through,” Ilya said.

“It is superficial.”

“That is not a medical category.”

“It is now.”

Ilya pulled the bandage tight. “You have a hearing in the morning.”

“I know.”

“You could sleep.”

“So could you.”

“I’m not the one waiting to learn whether the city wants me hanged.”

“The city wants several things.”

“Yes,” Ilya said. “That is the trouble.”

A young voice came from the stairwell.

“Are you really the Bellmaker?”

The guard stepped between Mara and the speaker. A girl stood three steps above them, thin and mud-streaked, with a blanket around her shoulders. A brass tag hung from her neck, its number scratched nearly smooth.

“I told you to stay with the shelter group,” the guard said.

“My brother is on the list.”

“Go back.”

The girl looked past him. “Is it true?”

Mara set down her wrench.

“What have you heard?”

“That you rang the bells and drowned South Hook.”

“Some of it is true.”

The guard glanced at her. “You don’t have to—”

“Did you ring them?” the girl asked.

“Yes.”

“Did you kill the people?”

Mara felt the old answer waiting. I caused it. It was true, and it was not all the truth.

“I made a choice I knew could cause a catastrophe,” she said. “I ignored a warning. My actions helped create the flood that killed people in South Hook and other districts.”

The girl gripped her tag.

“The Council blocked rescue routes,” Mara continued. “They weakened the southern seawall and protected the northern basins. They had plans to abandon people before the bells rang. That is also true.”

“Then who killed my brother?”

Mara looked at the scratched number.

“I don’t know enough to give you one name.”

“You know your name.”

“Yes.”

“Say it.”

“Mara Venn.”

“Not Bellmaker?”

“That is what they called me.”

“Is it what you are?” The girl took another step down. “Are you a hero or a monster?”

The question moved through the stairwell. Aven stopped working. Ilya watched Mara without blinking.

Mara had spent twelve years preparing for hatred. Hatred gave the condemned a place to stand. She had spent the past weeks resisting the opposite temptation: to become useful enough that usefulness might be mistaken for innocence.

“Neither,” she said.

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is the answer I can live with.”

“Can you?”

Mara looked at her bandaged hands. “I don’t know.”

The girl’s face tightened with disappointment.

“My brother’s name is Oren,” she said. “They wrote his number, but not his name.”

“Tell the registrar.”

“I did.”

“Tell them again. Stand there while they write it. Make them read it back.”

“You’re not writing it?”

Mara reached for the slate at her belt, then stopped. The name belonged to the girl before it belonged to Mara.

“No,” she said. “It belongs to you first.”

The girl climbed back toward the shelter group.

“Tell them he was Oren,” Mara called. “Not only a number.”

After the girl left, Ilya said, “You could have written it.”

“Yes.”

“You could have made certain.”

“I cannot make certain for everyone.”

“No,” Ilya said. “You can’t.”

At dusk they brought Mara to the upper maintenance room. The first warning bell hung from a blackened frame. Its lower rim had cracked during the engine surge, and the clapper was bent. A red cloth had been tied around the bell to catch falling fragments.

Oris had drawn the repair sequence on the wall.

Mara studied it. “Your third brace is too high.”

Oris, pale from exhaustion, glanced over. “I know.”

“It will pull against the frame.”

“I know.”

“Then why is it there?”

“The lower bracket failed.”

“Shift the weight.”

“Show me.”

He handed her the chalk. Mara marked the alteration and explained the load transfer. He interrupted twice. A guard asked her to repeat the pressure estimate. A woman from Lantern Ward demanded to know why the northern signal had been tested before the southern one. Aven objected that the eastern grate was not yet clear.

Mara answered each question.

No one accepted her instruction without asking why. When someone disagreed, she did not treat the disagreement as sabotage.

At last the bell was freed from its collar. The replacement clapper had been made from the axle of a market cart. Mara fitted it through the bell’s throat and secured the retaining ring. Her hands throbbed beneath their bandages. Twice she dropped a pin; twice someone else retrieved it.

She had once believed control meant never dropping anything.

“Test strike,” she said.

No one moved.

“Who is authorized?” the guard asked.

Mara looked toward the tribunal clerk, who sat at a table with the repair conditions: open schematics, interrupted authority, witnesses from the affected districts, public review.

“The crew,” the clerk said. “With witness consent.”

The Lantern Ward woman stepped forward. “Do it. If it fails, write that it failed.”

Mara pulled the cord.

The bell spoke.

The cracked rim gave the note a rough edge, but the sound traveled down the shaft, across the water, through the stone.

For one breath there was silence.

Then the eastern bell answered.

Three strikes. A pause. Three more.

A bell from the upper city joined it. Then one from the north. Deep below the engine, something older answered with the same rhythm.

The Lantern Ward woman began to cry.

Mara climbed down. The clerk recorded the time.

“Does it belong to every district now?” the young guard asked.

Mara looked through the open doorway toward Veyr’s scattered lights. Some shone from rooftops and boats. Others burned behind windows in streets still smelling of mud. The southern districts remained dark.

“No,” she said. “Not yet.”

He waited.

“It belongs to every district only if every district can hear it, question it, and answer back.”

He wrote that down.

The tribunal chamber stood across the Old Customs Exchange behind temporary canvas walls. Mara went there after midnight, escorted by two guards. Inside, the benches were empty. The old judges’ platform had been stripped of its banners, leaving a blank canvas behind it.

Tomas’s evidence case lay on the first bench. He had left it there for the morning. The leather was stiff with dried water, one corner marked by blood from his shoulder.

Mara did not touch it.

His testimony belonged to him. Hers belonged to her. Neither confession could carry the other across the river.

Outside, voices moved through the Exchange.

Some demanded her execution. Some demanded that she be put back to work. Others wanted a new authority that promised never to resemble the old one. Many simply sat beside the dead and said nothing.

Ilya appeared at the far end of the corridor carrying a folded blanket.

“You should sleep,” she said.

“So should you.”

“I already gave you that instruction.”

“I remember.”

She handed her the blanket. “They have not decided what you are.”

“They should not decide what I am.”

“They will decide what happens to you.”

“Yes.”

“Are you afraid?”

Mara could have lied. “Yes.”

Ilya nodded. “Good.”

“Good?”

“It means you’re not trying to turn the hearing into another machine.”

Mara looked at the blank canvas. “I still want to know the result.”

“That is not the same as controlling it.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is worse.”

She sat outside the chamber. No one had barred the door. No one had invited her through. That was the condition she had asked for: no lock mistaken for judgment, no freedom mistaken for absolution.

At dawn, the repaired network would begin carrying public warnings. The crews had agreed on one signal for open shelter, another for blocked routes, another for rising pressure. They had not agreed what to call the ancient answering rhythm. For now it remained unnamed.

Mara heard the city waking: oars against flooded streets, boots on timber bridges, tools striking metal at the tower.

Then the bell sounded.

Three strikes.

A pause.

Three strikes.

Mara did not rise. She did not touch the cord. She did not tell the sound where to go.

It passed through the open gate and entered every district that could receive it.

When the tribunal doors opened, Mara was still waiting outside—not for forgiveness, not for a name, not for a place among heroes or monsters, but for the consequence of what she had chosen and what others had chosen after her.

Her hands rested in her lap, scarred and unpardoned.

She listened.
